utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the question of Mr. Lilic's return, his lawyer would like to address Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAPONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be allowed to say a few words, with respect to the end of Mr. Lilic's testimony, Mr. Lilic responded to the Court order for the first time last year. However, the conditions weren't ripe for testimony then. He has been informed that -- he was now informed he is invited to testify next June, on the 16th of June, and on Thursday, the 19th of June. Bearing in mind the fact that the Prosecution completed its examination-in-chief on time, and that the cross-examination of the accused is under the supervision and control of the Trial Chamber, in keeping with Rule 90(F) and (H) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and as by having a schedule for today, and by disposing of our time today, we are able to ensure a footing of equality for both parties and additional cross-examination. We should like to ask, with the Court's indulgence and all due respect, that the testimony of Mr. Lilic be completed by the end of today. Mr. Lilic has kindly requested that you take into consideration the facts presented by him as well as his business engagements and others, personal reasons included, and unfortunately, this makes it impossible for him to come back to the Tribunal to testify at a later date. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May I address the Court on this matter. I think this is really an unwarranted interference in the conduct of the court business. It's a matter for this Court to decide how appropriate it is for a witness to give evidence, and the length of time, balancing the interests of the need for expedition and the need for a fair trial. The Court knows that Mr. Milosevic is very concerned to put his case in full to this witness. He's an important witness. He has been mentioned continuously throughout various significant events in relation to the trial. The Prosecutor has an advantage in being able to get his information and facts quickly and directly before the Court through expeditious rules of procedure. But for Mr. Milosevic, it is a harder task in cross-examining and asking questions that require more time for a witness of this nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We are very concerned. We have to tell you about interference in the way that we run this trial. But of course, we'll hear what you've got to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANCESKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should just like to make a technical remark and correction. I see that in the transcript it states that when Counsel Saponjic addressed the Trial Chamber, it also says that I addressed you because it says "Mr. Panceski". That's my name, so I'd just like to make that clear and correct that for the transcript. The name, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That's a perfectly proper intervention. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There should be proper time for cross-examination of a witness of this importance, and we, for that reason, will permit the accused the extra session this afternoon in order for him to conclude his cross-examination. It is, of course, a matter for the Trial Chamber whether the witness comes back or not. We bear in mind, though, his difficulties, the fact that he has made himself available to give evidence here, and that shouldn't be to the exclusion of any other considerations. However, it will be a matter essentially for the Prosecution whether they wish this witness to return or not. It's a matter whether they insist upon, or think, that re-examination is a worthwhile exercise. So we will lead the matter in that way. We are not fully constituted at the moment, so we cannot give a full ruling. When we are fully constituted, if there is an application made to us in respect of the witness, we'll consider it. Meanwhile, Mr. Milosevic, you've got today to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We were talking about events of 1995, and you explained certain aspects of those events. Do you happen to remember that there was a whole brigade of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, Izetbegovic's, asked by mediators for my agreement and permission, for them to cross the Drina River and find their salvation in Serbia, and there were 840 men, that's what the brigade numbered, a whole brigade. And they asked simply refuge in the onslaught that was -- to destroy them. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that event. I don't recall the details, but I do remember the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that we gave permission for them to cross over the river, the only condition stipulated was that they should cross without bearing arms, and we put them up in a police camp, they had physicians to attend to them. They were given food, et cetera. And the same day, or rather the next day, we sent representatives of diplomatic missions to visit them, the Red Cross and so on, for them to see who these people were. And for them to see that they were being well cared for.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think there was a general sentiment that we were all very satisfied with this humane gesture on our part towards the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, I have a report from the Politika paper about that event, so I don't want to waste any time on that now, as you agree. And I'm sure you'll remember that at that time, both sides asked that we return them, send them back. When I say "both sides," I mean the leadership of Republika Srpska wanted us to hand them over to them for them to be exchanged later on, and via international intermediaries, the leadership led by Alija Izetbegovic wanted us to return these men to him. But I refused to grant my permission to both sides, and the explanation I gave was that I didn't want to send them back because they were under my protection. And as far as the army was concerned, the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, from where they had come, I did not have any evidence showing that they were volunteers in that army and so I didn't want to send the men back to them either. I wanted to ensure that, as they were well taken care of, had recuperated, were clothed, fed, and sent to some neutral country from whence each of them could decide of their own free will whether they would go back, return there, or whether they would go to cousins in Australia, America, Germany or anywhere else in the world. Wasn't that how it was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was your position which was publicly declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then after a fairly lengthy period of time, and they weren't treated as prisoners of war at all, they were treated as refugees, we transferred them to Hungary where they were taken over by the International High Commission for Refugees, and then they enabled them to go off to different parts of the world if they so desired. So was it quite clear, then, that when the soldiers of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army are seeking refuge in Serbia, that there can be no mention of the fact that they were seeking refuge with an aggressor side, as they wanted to ascribe this to us on a political level?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And I can freely add that Serbia, as to its ethnic composition, was almost the same as the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was, ethnically speaking, and that during the war in Bosnia and Croatia, there were all kinds of ethnic groups living in Yugoslavia, or rather, Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned, or rather, you were asked by Mr. Nice something with respect to Abdic. He asked you whether you had seen Abdic in Belgrade, I think. Now, do you remember that the visit was broadcast on television?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said in response to that question that the media covered the visit, and it was covered by the information media as a whole, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that Abdic at that time set up an autonomous province of Western Bosnia and concluded a peace agreement both with Republika Srpska and with Croatia, that is to say, he wanted to have this enclave and preserve it and pull it out of all kinds of war activities and to continue to cooperate normally. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Abdic did make a statement to that effect, or a similar one. I can't say precisely what he said, but I think he told the information media in Belgrade the same thing, words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you recall that an agreement was even signed between them that took place in the Presidency of Serbia building, and I signed the agreement as a witness? I witnessed the agreement as it was signed.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as far as that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned, for the time being, the war stopped there in those parts, and the relationships between the Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, but unfortunately, the 5th Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, under the command of Atif Dudakovic, continued the war. Now, do you remember there were many events, many atrocities carried out by the members of that corps against the Muslims precisely, those who were advocates of peace, who supported peace in the autonomous province of Western Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information we received, it was not only the 5th Corps but the Muslim leadership from Sarajevo, too, which was highly dissatisfied with Mr. Fikret Abdic's position, the position he had taken, and it was precisely against that Muslim population that the repressions were most severe, after the proclamation of the autonomy of Western Bosnia, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember that in fact it was at those first elections for the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to the war that Fikret Abdic was a personality who won the majority of votes, more than Alija Izetbegovic, and he was to have been the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina by rights?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that could be seen from the official reports and from the information media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, he ceded that right to Izetbegovic, and the supremacy. He said he was a businessman and not a politician, and that he didn't want to delve in political matters and he just stayed on as a member of the Presidency. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Later on, this led to fatal consequences, and you will remember, I'm sure, the extent to which the Islamic declaration was made use of and generally the extent to which the doors were opened to Islamic fundamentalism at that time in Bosnia-Herzegovina when Izetbegovic came to head the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I personally think that that was one of the greatest evils that engulfed Bosnia-Herzegovina, the presence of the Muslamic [sic] or -- rather, Muslim or Islamic fundamentalism and the enormous resources that flowed in as assistance, monetary assistance to Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We had a witness here testifying several days before you here, and among other things he said that we extended aid and assistance to Republika Srpska and Srpska Krajina, and we discussed that subject yesterday in this courtroom, too. I asked the witness: "All right, what do you find strange in that, that the Serbs should help --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can't comment on what some other witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on, then, to another area. But I think I can ask the witness whether he knows and whether it was challenged at all that the Muslim side in the war received aid and assistance from a whole series of countries and states, including a large group of the Mujahedin volunteers and so on who took part in the atrocities perpetrated against both the Serbs and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that the witness is well placed to answer this, in view of the post he occupied. He received information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not challenged or contested as is not the presence of certain fundamentalists and their identification on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. Even in the combat units of Alija Izetbegovic. I think there are very valid and strong arguments in the army of Yugoslavia pointing to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true and correct -- now we're talking about Kosovo -- that in our leadership, it was common knowledge amongst our leaders that America was publicly advocating an agreement between Serbia and the Kosovo Albanians, whereas through its secret diplomacy and intelligence work, it was delving intensively in the reorganisation of the KLA, which already in September and October of 1998 had been thwarted.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the intelligence information that we received, and information from the centres where Albanian terrorists were being trained, there was a great role there by them on that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you consider at the time that they were preparing the KLA for the spring onslaught?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a matter for the witness. Maybe some evidence about it in due course which we can consider, but the opinion of the witness on that is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I think that it is a proper question for the witness because we have his vision of the situation here, and it is a document which relates to -- actually, it's a letter in which he presents all these aspects, and the number 04449622, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the federal government, the signatory is Zoran Lilic. And in that letter, he puts views forward that he talked about. He was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put the letter to him if you've got a copy of it, so much the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 31.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they do have a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have his copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, let's just clear one point up first, please. Is it true that you endeavoured to give an overall picture, a comprehensive picture here on the basis of all the information you had at your disposal, the military services, the security services, the public security services, information provided to you from the foreign affairs department, the service for information of the foreign affairs department, or rather the centre for the collection of information? So all the information that was made available to you, you studied all of that and endeavoured to make a summary and precis of it and condense it into a review and report of the basic assessments, positions, et cetera. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter that I addressed to you round about the 20th of November was compiled on the basis of all the knowledge that I had, intelligence information, information provided from different services, intelligence from abroad and all the sources that you mentioned, but also on the basis of an insight of what was happening on the ground. And I think that it is very easy to document all this with JNA documents, SID documents, and calling in other witnesses if need be and if the Court so desires to present and document these views.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I omitted to state that, and you're quite right partially when you say that apart from all the information that was coming in on that basis, this was also the result of your own visits to Kosovo in agreement with me, with the corresponding representatives of the police, army, local organisations and bodies and so on and so forth. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, at the time, was the assessment that was made this: That they would be preparing a terrorist organisation called the KLA for its spring operations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of the knowledge we had, that was quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true and correct that it was our conviction and belief that they would use their -- they would wield influence on Albanian leaders, and you mentioned Rugova by name here, but I'm sure you had others in mind as well, that they would procrastinate in their negotiations, take one step forward, one step back and to try and buy time because the KLA was in a very poor state at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that was precisely the time when the terrorist army of Kosovo, the KLA or UCK, whatever you like to call it, I don't want to say that it had been destroyed, but it was in a general state of disarray, and facing ultimate -- an ultimate breakdown, so that the assessment here is quite correct, not only by Mr. Rugova, but by most of the Albanian leaders, and they tried to unite them around one goal because they were disunited to a certain extent, even the Albanian leaders at that time and they were trying to rally them around one goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the assessment made and the evaluation given of the ultimate goal of the Clinton administration was to bring in the NATO forces to Kosovo and Metohija? Is that right? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my impression on the basis on all the intelligence I had and that is what I set out in my letter to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Tell me this please: Is it correct that Hill, then, and Christopher Hill at that time was the US ambassador to Macedonia and in charge of these direct contacts in Kosovo, is it true that he made offers to the KLA by way of various modified solutions that go outside the framework of the agreement reached between Holbrooke and myself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, at that time it was Mr. Sainovic who negotiated or talked to Mr. Hill at that time. This information is what I received from people from the actual area, even people who were involved with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, then, that the main goal of the administration was to make an external ring around Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this letter, I tried to answer that question in particular. As I provided information about the number of soldiers in Macedonia and also, according to this source that was highly relevant, what the number of personnel that would come in would be. And if this is placed on a map, then one can see that this actually closes the ring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the buildup of foreign troops in Albania was not aimed at stopping incursions by terrorists, but to manipulate refugees, and once there's a conflict they would cross over to Albania and in this way create conditions for portraying some kind of a humanitarian catastrophe?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I wrote this letter or this report or this piece of information for you, this seemed to be a sound assumption. But later on, it proved to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the orders, instructions, and activities that took place during the NATO aggression against Yugoslavia in terms of the KLA, what the KLA said to the population, instructing them to leave the territory of Kosovo en masse and go to Albania, Macedonia, and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was not in a position to be in Kosovo and Metohija, but I was aware of such orders that were issued. The information I have shows that this is a fact. Actually, before the NATO bombing began, the number of refugees in Macedonia and in Albania altogether did not exceed the number of 35.000. After the NATO bombing started, according to UNHCR figures, so these are not figures that come from our sources but from UN sources, this number went up. And if I -- if my memory still serves me well, it went up to about 780.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it quite clear that at that time, they were not fleeing before any kind of Serb operations, or that some kind of process of their deportation had been organised by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure this witness can answer that. He wasn't there at the time. It is a crucial issue which the Trial Chamber will have to determine. And his opinion on it may not assist.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not asking the witness for his opinion, Mr. May, I'm asking him about the facts that he was aware of at the time. At that time, he was Deputy Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can't say as to the facts. He cannot say as to what happened. He can merely tell us, and he has been allowed so far, but this is a crucial issue, to say what reports he had on your side. Now, he can't say of his own knowledge what caused the Albanians to become refugees. And as I say, that's a matter we're going to have to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Lilic, do you know why the Albanians became refugees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I'm not going to allow that question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, it seems that questions are allowed when a witness is brought in who heard and saw something in a village in Bosnia, and it's not allowed to put questions to the former president and Deputy Prime Minister of Yugoslavia who was indeed competent to give answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Were you in Kosovo at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you have any direct evidence yourself which you can give on this particular issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I have the knowledge that I obtained from others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, from second-hand sources. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Milosevic, what he obtained from some other source isn't going to assist us. If you want to call evidence as to what happened in Kosovo, of course, you're able to do that. But for this witness to say "we received these reports" doesn't seem to me to add anything. Well, I'm going to allow this question. Did you talk to any of these refugees yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. May. At that time, I was not in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we proceed, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that at that time, Albania, and I'm referring to the end of 1998, became the logistic base for terrorists and that it was used for opening channels from Albania in order to bring in terrorists and weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and we received daily reports about the quantities of weapons seized. There were increasingly frequent clashes at the border towards Albania. Quite a few people got killed, terrorists, and also there was shooting against members of the Yugoslav army. We also were aware of camps on the other side of the border where terrorists were trained. According to our intelligence reports, that's the way it was, and this information can be verified. In those bases, there were about 5.000 terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for verifiers, it correct that then the British and the Americans were covering the border and creating a linkup with Macedonia and Albania where there were NATO forces as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our border units, I think, reported every day about the presence of the verifiers that you've just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Similar information, that is to say, from similar sources that are reliable enough, is the kind of information that you received in respect to the first question that has to do with refugees, the one that Mr. May will not let you answer. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I respect the position taken by Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm just bearing in mind the fact that the Deputy Prime Minister does not go to actual places where things happen and to talk to each and every verifier. A Deputy Prime Minister has reliable information from the appropriate services and agencies. Is it true that it was agreed in Germany that Bukoshi would buy weapons amounting to 12 million deutschmarks?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a well-known fact, and later through a mistake made by the Albanian side this appeared in the local media. This is an intelligence report of ours, though, and these weapons were in Kosovo. I do not want to prejudge anything. I don't want to say where the weapons came from, but the weapons were there, and they belonged to East Germany before the reunification of Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Berisha, the former president of Albania, controlled the north of Albania, took it upon himself to organise terrorists and to send them in from Albania?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our information, and I think the army of Yugoslavia does have these intercepts of conversation. Berisha did hold this part of Albania, and even after all the unrest in Albania, I think that he was actually in charge of all the weapons reserves that happened to be in Albania at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to all the information that was made accessible to you, were some sophisticated weapons supposed to be brought in by the verifiers, too? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it clear that the verification mission of the OSCE was being abused for reanimating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is only your opinion, and this is no doubt the intelligence which your side had and the reports which your side had. It really is of no great assistance for us to have this retold. You've put it to the verifiers and they have denied it. We'll have to tell what the truth was. If you've got some direct evidence about it, of course, you can call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the new channel for bringing in terrorists was via Sarajevo and then via Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And what was most interesting was, and it can be seen from this letter that was underlined, that regular buses were used for this. And they went through Belgrade in groups numbering from three to five men. That's really interesting, and that's how they went from Kosovo, and that's how they came from the airport in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They came in groups of two or three men just as passengers on regular bus lines, and then they were transferred as civilians and then they were equipped and armed down there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And through Macedonia, Skopje, they also went into Kosovo. So that is the information we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that already then, in 1998, they were armed and they even had Hamber stingers and other weapons with 2.000 metre ranges, weapons that could only be obtained with the assistance of certain services of other countries?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can talk about the first fact, and that is that they did have such snipers. And that was seen on the casualties on our side, that is to say, that they did have these weapons which in some situations and in some of the operations carried out by our anti-terrorist units, such weapons were actually seized.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was the estimate made then that it was -- the Albanian leadership was buying time so that NATO could build up its forces in Macedonia and Albania and so that they could get enough weapons to the terrorists and that they could link up the territories under their control?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for such activities, and the objectives of such efforts made by them, this was something that was pointed to by all the information that I had the possibility to see, and this coincides with what I said here, with everything that happened in March when the NATO aggression started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it clear on the basis of all these facts that the international community would not react in order to stop the activities of terrorists? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was evident in the field itself. The terrorists behaved as if they were on their own territory and as if the Serb side were the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, you then proposed that a special staff be set up for organising special armed forces apart from the MUP and the army, however, is it correct that the MUP and the army had their own chains of command and that a third chain of command could not be organised?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the army of Yugoslavia, there were special units which could carry out the task that I had proposed. And within the police, there were special units that were very well equipped. My proposal was to set up a third special unit that would only deal with anti-terrorist activities. Of course, obviously your assessment was different. But the fact remains that units from the MUP and the army of Yugoslavia did have their chain of command. Of course, this unit could have been set up within one of these groups, either the army of Yugoslavia or the MUP. My assessment was that at all costs, the terrorists should be broken up by the month of March. And if this fails, then an ultimatum should be delivered to them, quite literally they should be surrounded and then operations should be launched against them, and of course the international community would have to be notified thereof. So that we would avoid subsequent problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, the international community had its own verification mission in Kosovo. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but my idea was that we should inform them about all activities taking place against the terrorists so that we would avoid any kind of speculations. Another thing that I consider to be particularly important was to provide additional security for the border in order to stop arms smuggling, infiltration of weapons, and as you know, with your consent, I travelled to some countries to talk about possible electronic surveillance and security for the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well. We tried to secure the border as best we could. Now, let us briefly move on to this document that was presented here, Perisic's letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you have the tab number for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have a copy myself, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look now. Since you provided some explanations in relation to this letter of his, I noticed during the examination-in-chief that you first said that you did not wish to comment upon Perisic's letter because it was his letter. But Mr. Nice insisted that you do comment upon certain matters. So now, I would like to deal with some questions related to that. First of all, is it quite clear that this is a mere smokescreen in order to dodge responsibility for what was supposed to be done in line with the duties that the army has in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm hesitating to object to any of these questions for obvious reasons, because if the accused thinks he's getting favourable answers from the witness, I don't want to be standing in the way. But I wonder about the formation of that last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's an interpretation of the letter. Can the witness not put an interpretation on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a matter for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For what it's worth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For what it's worth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, you're being asked about this letter. If you can give your own view of it, if you consider it worth giving, of course, you may, if you agree with the accused's interpretation. But if not, just say so. Or if, indeed, you think you can't give a useful opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hardly agree with what Mr. Milosevic said, that this is a smokescreen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let us examine it and each of the allegations it contains. Is it true that Perisic was advocating -- we'll come to those marginal matters later. But he was advocating basically for the introduction of a state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said. There was another letter accompanying this letter. I don't know whether it is included in these documents. And from which it can be seen that Perisic was insisting on the introduction of a state of emergency in a part of the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or better still, Republic of Serbia, to acquire legitimacy for the use of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true, and I think that you're quite qualified to answer this question in view of the position you held, that no state of emergency is required for the army to react to terrorist attacks, which we had established, were being resorted against members of the army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic insisted that the army react in that way in the area of responsibility of the army, that is, in the border belt which was relatively narrow, depth-wise, and I think by decision of the federal government, it was later extended to 5 kilometres. But that the use of the army, together with the anti-terrorist units that were in Kosovo, should be given appropriate orders through the institution of a state of emergency. However, objectively, in view of the reports that I had occasion to see in writing given by him, realising that his insistence with you and your approval for me to visit Kosovo and Metohija on two occasions to examine the situation there was really to confirm that most roads had been blocked by the terrorists and could not be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that on the basis of the relevant regulations, the army even in peacetime, may be used to secure communication lines, in the case of natural disasters, to respond to the struggle against terrorism, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the peacetime conditions that you refer to, absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So to respond to terrorism, no state of emergency was needed. And do you remember, according to the information which I hope you had access to at the time, that in Kosovo and Metohija, the security was jeopardised of the citizens by terrorist activities in a total of 213 inhabited places, out of a total of 1.413 inhabited places in Kosovo, which means 1/6th roughly. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but it is a fact that there were very many places where this was true. And in fact, most of the villages were left without any Serbs under pressure of Albanian terrorists, and even the Albanians themselves who had lived there for centuries moved from the Metohija area of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were 1.200 places in which there were no terrorist attacks, and that the introduction of a state of emergency was not necessary in order to respond to terrorism as we have noted, and such a state of emergency would have been a blow to civil rights and freedoms in 6/7ths of the territory in relation to 1/7th that was exposed to terrorist attacks. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was your judgement, and you had the right to have such a judgement at the time. And the Supreme Defence Council of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had the right to say that. But it is a fact that the army would have provided more logistics and be able to activate larger units, to move artillery units and to act together with the police. For all that to be possible, a state of emergency was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't the best evidence the fact that without a state of emergency, the KLA had actually been broken up, and that the verification mission arrived by agreement, and the presence of the army was reduced to three main strategic crossroads at the level of a company with the exception of the army and the barracks?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we're talking here about General Perisic's letter and the reasons for that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The reasons are obvious, to justify himself to his external tutors recording the instructions he received as confirmed by subsequent course of events when he was arrested for espionage?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know, Mr. Milosevic, that Perisic, while I was president, was working for any foreign service because I personally would have arrested him if I had known. If something happened later on, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Have we cleared up the point that it is the duty of the army, even in peacetime conditions, when it comes to lines of communication - when I say that, I mean roads, main roads, traffic communications, the struggle against terrorism, et cetera - that this is covered by the regulations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, securing the territory beyond the border area is the duty of the Ministry of the Interior. Certainly the army should react if any member of the army is in jeopardy, but those are individual cases. It could not entail any kind of frontal engagement of the army without that state of emergency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in the constitution of Yugoslavia, it says in Article 133 -- I don't wish to offend you by asking you whether you know it; I just wish to refresh your memory. It says the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has an army which defends the sovereignty, territory, independence, and constitutional order. Therefore, the army is there to defend the territory, sovereignty, independence, and constitutional order were the territory, or at least one of these elements, and I believe all of them were actually in jeopardy due to terrorist activities in that time in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely not at issue. I'm not offended at all. I'm very familiar with this article of the constitution. May I finish. I know this article very well. But also, there is the law on defence and the law of the army of Yugoslavia which clearly defines when and how units of the army are to be used. Of course, the engagement of the army in accordance with the decision of the Supreme Defence Council may be ordered by the president of the Federal Republic without a state of emergency. And that is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why, then, was it necessary for Perisic to write a letter explaining that what can be done without a state of emergency can only be done with a state of emergency? Have we agreed that this could be done without a state of emergency and that this allegation that it can only be done with a state of emergency is not right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not wish to interpret Perisic. If he had an adequate order, he should have used the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we have here a discussion about what the army can do in peacetime and in a state of emergency. These are constitutional issues and the Chamber has already said that the witness may answer to the extent that he can on these issues. But to my mind, it raises again the question of the need for a constitutional expert. You did produce one and the Chamber did not allow him to give evidence, but in the Chamber's view, it is clearly necessary for the Prosecution to provide evidence on constitutional matters in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the Chamber ruled out the constitutional expert at that stage on certain topics. I'm not sure whether it particularly ruled it out on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not on all topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not on all topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On the Kosovo-related topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The way it was expressed, I have to go back and look at it. I'm not sure this is expressly ruled out. I can simply remind the Chamber that, for whatever reason, finding somebody at the time who was prepared to give evidence in this trial, with the appropriate constitutional law credentials, was not easy. People were, frankly, on several occasions, afraid to do so. Now, we made available to you a constitutional expert, and I was, of course, amused -- not amused. I permitted myself a wry smile at a later occasion when there was a discussion in relation to Mr. Babovic about who was to be preferred as to the legal matters on which he was speaking as between the Judge of the Court and him. Never mind. It was a wry smile. We may be able to find another constitutional law expert with suitable credentials, but the one we have been in a position to offer is Mr. Kristan. He may be able to deal with this topic, because I think it was revocation of Kosovo's autonomy that was the only topic expressly ruled out. And of course, if the accused wishes to raise constitutional matters with a qualified Prosecution witness, then although we may have been denied the opportunity to raise those issues with the witness, it is open to the accused to raise them with him himself, especially since he knows what his answers will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What it amounts to is this: That the original expert was permitted to give evidence on constitutional issues, apart from the matter in which it was deemed that he might be said to have had an interest and there was a ruling. But that was a fairly narrow issue, and the rest of his report, as I recollect, dealt with broader issues, and that was not excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct. And indeed, it's our intention to call him back, as I made clear at the time, but it will probably be in the autumn. Now, what I can attempt to do - and I will discuss this with the team later to see when we can timetable his return - is to have him back as soon as may be so that we can see how much of his report we can make available to you, and discover from the accused how much in addition he may put in himself. Then if there is a margin not covered, it will give us a couple of months to go and find somebody else who may be able to help. And of course, things may be a little different in the light of the regime change that's happened, but we had very considerable difficulties in finding somebody to come and assist you with the appropriate credentials on the first occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We encourage you in those efforts, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think we've exhausted this topic as to the state of emergency as far as this witness is concerned. Now, if you've got any other questions about the letter, the Perisic letter, you can, of course, ask them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you allowed Mr. Nice to smile, allow me to smile too, wryly. I didn't object that Mr. Nice's witness for constitutional matters testifies about Kosovo whatever he wants to. In fact, it suits me even better to refute such testimony. It gives me greater satisfaction to refute the evidence of witnesses brought here by Mr. Nice than to try and prove this through my own witnesses, which I will certainly not fail to do. You yourself ruled that this witness should not testify about constitutional matters linked to Kosovo, and I wish to remind you that I did not object at all. On the contrary, it would be a pleasure for me to confront my arguments with his. But let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder, may I try and save time, invite the Chamber to reconsider its ruling in light of the express indication of the accused. When fully constituted, the Chamber might decide that constitutes a new fact upon which, unusually, it could reconsider matters. But nevertheless, I will have the topic in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I very much doubt it. Of course, we will have a look at it again. I very much doubt it. There was a particular reason why that evidence was excluded, and it had to do with the witness's involvement in the very activity in which he was going to give evidence about as an expert. And it was from that point of view that the Chamber excluded the evidence as not properly that of an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I quite understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, did you have occasion to look at this reminder for the members of the army of Yugoslavia engaged in the area swept by sabotage and terrorist activities, this was the whole area which was swept by sabotage and terrorist activities, passed in June 1998 by the general staff of the army of Yugoslavia? I will give you a copy to look at. And my question is whether you had occasion to see it. And it says here --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I get a copy. May I have the document to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is 02093686. It is page 1. I received it in this set of documents which the opposite side is providing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us find that. Is it in the binder, first of all? The reference to June 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The title page, 020936865, and it has the coat of arms of Yugoslavia. I see they received this from the general staff. It says: "Military secret, for internal use, reminder for members of the army."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it? What is the document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a document of the general staff. Maybe the witness can explain it for you. He's quite qualified to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we can find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a reminder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us find it, a reminder, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until they find it, I can read some excerpts. Signed by the general staff, so it is a kind of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not in the binder, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us see if we can find it first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The numbers given are not in the binder. The only June -- was it 19th of June? I can't remember. Document of 1968... There are a couple of documents, 25 and -- I don't think it's those. We are looking through for other documents disclosed to the accused. If he tells us what it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, while it's being looked for, you can read it, Mr. Milosevic, and we'll see if we can get on in that way. Mr. Lilic, we don't seem to have the document at the moment. The accused can read what parts he wants to you, and then you can have a look at it before you have to answer. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll let him have a look at it. Of course I will, yes. So the title page, the first page, I've already indicated the general staff of the army, military secret, internal. It's an aide memoire. I assume they could have tabled this on the basis of a government order, and they did so here, for members of the army engaged in the area engulfed by sabotage and terrorist operations and activities. And then they go on to say in point 1, the conduct of the members of the Yugoslav army and the units from jeopardising people, materiel, resources and facilities in the areas taken over by sabotage operations, so there's nothing else that is endangered but people, materiel, goods, facilities, and so on. And then it says should rebel terrorists sabotage and other armed units launch an attack, I don't want to enumerate it all, use all available men and materiel according to the principles of combat in order to defend yourselves successfully to thwart and rout the enemy. I apologise to the interpreters for reading so fast. I'll do my best to read slower. That means to use all available human resources and materiel resources based on the principles of units deployment in order to put up a successful defence and thwart and destroy the groups mentioned. In refuting an attack, ensure law and order, law and order should prevail. Unconditional implementation and execution of orders, and a responsible conduct. And preventing all unlawful conduct on the part of members of units and commands. Then it goes on to speak of the sabotage units to prevent their reconnaissance, abilities to effect reconnaissance, and so on and so forth. And then it goes on to say that in the struggle against the rebel terrorist sabotage units and other hostile armed groups, in addition to other things, the following principles should be adhered to in order to search these groups, attack them, destroy sabotage units, do not use smaller units than companies. And it says company/battery. That is, in two branches of the army. And that means not to use and deploy small units such as platoons, but that the units deployed should number at least one company. And from enemy groups, built up areas and so on, after cautioning them, use artillery for the selective destruction of enemy and facilities from which fire has already come. In deploying the units of the artillery and tank units, and then it says a tank company in brackets, strengthen them and reinforce them by infantry units, engineers units and other units in conformity with the tasks undertaken. Used to encircle and block built-up areas and settlements, do not enter built-up areas with the units of the Yugoslav army in order to control communications and territory jeopardised through terrorist activity, use armoured mechanised units and necessary reinforcements if these are required. There is a grammatical error here but I'm reading out the way it says. [Indiscernible] are not allowed to enter into operation if the unit is not fully prepared to do so. Of course, the army acted upon these rules of procedure and principles in keeping with the provisions stipulated. All I'm saying is this has nothing to do with the state of emergency. Point 2 is to how the men should act if the diversionary and sabotage groups should attack because there was kidnapping of soldiers, ambushes, and so on. And then number 3, how to behave towards sabotage units when they are taken into custody and captured. Conduct therein. And it says that if sabotage units use weapons to defend themselves, then act in conformity with the rules and regulations. Once the sabotage units surrender their arms, conduct should be as follows: Anything involving terrorist acts should be confiscated, any weapons they might have, and the commanders of units have the right to interrogate individuals on military matters. Intelligence reports are filed as to the crimes committed, and they can be held in custody for three days, for a maximum of three days, after which they will have to be prosecuted and taken to court, et cetera. And particular stress is laid on the fact that nobody can kill any POWs or inflict physical attempts on them. Respect should be shown towards women and children of the terrorist group members as required by their sex and age, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters apologise, but the text was very fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'd like to say that you need to re-examine your approach to cross-examination. I have been looking at the screen, and the full-length of the screen has been gone through at least two times without a question coming from you. This is not -- it's not practical. We have limited time, and we take account of the fact that you are conducting your own defence. But I think you have to make a very serious effort to summarise matters and to put questions to the witness. After speaking for four, five, six minutes, the witness has probably forgotten what you started out with. I certainly have. And I have to follow it. As a rule of thumb, I would suggest that when you have spoken for about a minute, no longer than a minute, you should put a question. Look at the screen, if you see that you have -- there are two or three sentences that you have completed, the time has come for you to put a question because we have to follow the cross-examination. Please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've located the document. I don't know how long it will be before it's with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've located it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, it seems that good intentions can be understood wrongly. I quoted all this in view of the witness's competence and in order to save time, so I wanted to put it all to him at once, and then ask him the question. And I'll just end by saying that of course, special emphasis was laid on the fact that it was forbidden to act against anybody's human dignity for the POWs, the persons taken into custody and captured. But the title of this document, the date, in fact, is June 1998. There's no other date. It just says "June 1998" at the bottom. But that is sufficient. That is on the title page because President Perisic's letter is dated the 23rd of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that was at least one month before he wrote his -- well, I don't want to say what it was, given the qualifications. But with respect to this emergency situation, he is behaving totally in keeping with the provisions and rules stipulating the conduct of individuals on -- in the territory. So that is the document. I don't believe that Mr. Lilic doubts that I quoted verbatim from the text. That would be absurd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him look at it, and look through it, and ensure that that is as you said it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, first of all let the witness confirm that that is the document which is referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really don't need to read through the document. The document does seem to be authentic. I think it is the original used by the army of Yugoslavia as a sort of aide memoire. I don't know of this -- of the fact that this document was published. I assume that there was an order from the general staff prior to this document. Otherwise it couldn't have been issued. But we're not contesting the fact that a code of conduct does exist, the Supreme Defence Council does compile documents of this kind. And it does state that the army can be deployed and engaged under these stipulations and conditions. Of course, if there's not a state of emergency that has been proclaimed. So that is why this sort of reminder was compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I quoted Article 133 of the constitution according to the fact that FRY has an army and the constitutional provision for it to protect the sovereignty and territorial integrity and constitutional order of the country, therefore the country is duty-bound to act along those lines. And now a word of explanation with respect to the conduct of an army on a territory where there is sabotage activity. The army directly implements its constitutional obligations, so we can agree on that point and then move forward. So we can't speak of the unlawful and illegal deployment of the army in that area, can we?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the army can't decide on itself, regardless of Article 133. But as we're discussing experts in constitutional matters and issues, we can leave that to them, perhaps. It would be a good idea to have somebody who is an expert in military law. But it's not up to me to say so. I don't want to influence you one way or the other or make any proposals. It is quite certain that the army can be engaged, along with the corresponding orders and position taken by the Supreme Defence Council. That competence under Article 133 is not being challenged. But let me say that I never saw this document before. I'm seeing it for the first time now, and its contents apply to conduct, application, and all the other things that have been set out in detail. And it says June 1998. So those two documents speak for themselves. On the one hand, we're saying that these orders did not exist; this testifies to the reverse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not claiming one or the other. That is what is stated. So if the fact that people say that something is unlawful if a state of emergency is not in existence, this proves the opposite. Now, it says in rather pathetical terms, or rather Mr. Perisic has written this in rather pathetical terms --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Milosevic, but I just handed the letter back. May I be asked to be given the letter again, Mr. Perisic's letter, please. May I have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we go on to that, I've got here the letter produced by the accused -- any objection to this being exhibited? The letter produced by the accused. It's in B/C/S, I know, but presumably something disclosed by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Give it the next exhibit number. Yes, if you've got a translation, so much the better.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Defence Exhibit 146.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Otherwise, Mr. May, as you said a moment ago that this was disclosed by Mr. Nice, I should like to take advantage of this occasion to say that, as we can see, Mr. Nice can have access to documents, and does, from the archives of the Yugoslav government and the army of Yugoslavia, whereas my associates cannot. They do not have access to a single one and can't come by them, so I have to use only the documents that Mr. Nice's associates are able to come by, which is untenable, an untenable sort of relationship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's according to the rules. They're under an obligation, the Prosecution, to disclose to you any assistance, any matter which may assist you, anything which is exculpatory. They do. Yes, now let us go on with the Perisic letter, tab 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, a state of emergency, we've clarified that point up. He says that under these conditions, as professionals who have preserved the army and FRY, under these conditions, he considers it -- his merit for having done so. Now doesn't that sound - how shall I put this? - a little imbecile?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to add, it's not a proper question. Yes, anything else you want to ask about the letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's take it in order, one by one. He says "constant tendency to use the army outside the institutions of the system," and then he links this up to the state of the emergency. We cleared that point up. Otherwise, I'm sure you know - I hope you know, at least - and we have the law here, the law on defence, in fact, the competency and authority for a state of emergency, imminent war, war, and that is vested in the Assembly of Yugoslavia; isn't that right, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the proposal of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right, at the proposal of the government. And he says that he did contact the government, that the government did not respond to his requests, and I asked the Defence Minister something with respect to that, and the answer I was given is that there was no need for that because, according to the rules, and he indicated what was stated in the document itself, they could act along those lines. And he goes on to say: "Separation of units of the Yugoslav army outside the army of Yugoslavia," and then he goes on to say, or rather, to explain: "The Guards Brigade was separated from the army of Yugoslavia by your decision." Tell me, please, Mr. Lilic, who was in command of the Guards Brigade before this occurred by my decision, as General Perisic puts it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade was within the corps of the special units. It was subordinated to the special units corps directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what was the task of the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was more of a protocol nature, its tasks and assignments. Ceremonial, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume you know that the Guards Brigade also provides security for the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes; I didn't finish what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means to provide security for the residence of the president of the republic, his offices, the office of the president of the republic, and security for the Supreme Command. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, does the president of the republic, is he in command of the army both in peace and war pursuant to the Yugoslav constitution? Is he the Supreme Commander?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, pursuant to the constitution of Yugoslavia and Article 135 on the law of the army, Article 4 there, in that law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is it considered that if the Guards Brigade, which otherwise provides security for the head of state and is used for ceremonial matters is subordinated to the military cabinet of the president of the republic and is separated from the army of Yugoslavia, or is it within the composition of the army of Yugoslavia? Or is it perhaps the president of the republic which by virtue of the constitution commands the army and is this not considered part of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to have to interpret General Perisic. That is a thankless task. He would be best placed to say what he meant. May I finish what I was saying, Mr. Milosevic, please. Just a minute, please, may I take a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, we're talking about the disbanding of the special corps unit here, and placing it under the direct command of the Guards Brigade. Whether that was how it was when talking about the Guards Brigade, I really can't say. I don't know. However, we must respect the principle of subordination and singleness of command. You can't command the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And nor did I command it. But are you aware of the fact that never did the Guards Brigade at that material time that was attached or resubordinated to the military cabinet of the president of the republic and was not deployed for anything else except to provide security for the Supreme Command and the president of the republic and the ceremonial business that it engaged in. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say because I wasn't in a position to attend the Supreme Defence Council meetings. So I don't think -- although I just don't know. I don't believe that it was that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time has come for us to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have one question to ask with respect to the Guards Brigade, not to separate this issue from the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can see that on page 2 of his letter, he says that unless you do not have confidence in the chief of the general staff, unless you have no faith in the NGS, chief the general staff. That's what it says, that's what he says. Is that what Perisic wrote?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in that letter. But I was commenting on the letter believing in the authenticity of what was stated here. Any other interpretation on my part would be quite improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to adjourn now. Twenty minutes. Mr. Lilic, could you be back then, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. May I make three points very briefly. One, the document that the accused was referring to as showing that we had access to a particular archives came from an individual, it didn't come from an archive. Two, and -- four points then. The second point is that the last document produced has already been tendered as Exhibit 94, tab 72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In those circumstances, it may be convenient to delete it as a Defence exhibit. Tab 72; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, tab 72; 94, tab 72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Otherwise there's going to be confusion. So we'll delete it -- this is 146, I think was the last number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Delete that. Exhibit 94, tab 72. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Third point, we've considered the position: We will require to re-examine this witness. We falls into a particular category of witness of a kind we've had before where re-examination is really essential. No doubt the Chamber will -- perhaps I can invite the Chamber to make the position clear to the witness, particularly in light of the circumstances in which he is here, of which the Chamber is aware. Of course, we will accommodate with our other witnesses his convenience. Indeed, it is possible, I think, for a witness, if they catch the early flight from Belgrade, to be in and out in a day, surprisingly enough. And on that same topic, I can tell you that on the very early flight, or the early flight today, we are receiving from the authorities, as we understand it, the full records of the documents referred to on page 16 of the summary, the records of the state Council for Coordination, positions on state policy. Very important documents indeed. Now, they're coming up, having been provided. The Chamber will remember that the witness was able to identify them because he saw some left over from the period of Cosic's Presidency. We would be grateful, though there will be no re-examination, simply for an opportunity, once the documents arrive, for him to look at them and to confirm that they are in line with the documents that he saw, so then that the process of identification is complete and the documents can be processed in the usual way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. To make it plain, we will sit until 1.45, the usual time, today. We will deal with any future hearings for the witness in due course. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANCESKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, I do beg your pardon for interrupting. Just another brief correction. The documents that Mr. Nice referred to have been handed over by the national council, although these are documents that are part of the request for cooperation and on which the Trial Chamber ruled on the 12th of June, and it was rejected as too broad. The position of the National Council for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal is that these documents should be handed over as an act of courtesy. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, do you remember that the commander of the Guards Brigade in 1997, and that was General Bojovic, was appointed at the proposal of General Perisic to be ADC to the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember, because at that time, it was General Susic who was in charge of both duties. He was head of the military office of the president, and when necessary he was also ADC to the president. So at the proposal of the senior staff of the chief of general staff, General Bojovic was appointed ADC.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the end of Perisic's letter, it says in relation to the Guards Brigade, "unless you do not trust the chief of general staff." So what if I do not trust the chief of general staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know how to answer this question. It was the right of the Supreme Defence Council to appoint a new chief of staff, to keep the old one, to transfer him somewhere else. I don't think that this is a right that should be denied in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it is also not to be denied that General Perisic was dismissed according to legal procedure and in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had the opportunity of reading the minutes from the SDC, although he was not relieved of his duty by consensus. If I'm not mistaken, Mr. Djukanovic was against this, but this does not alter the legitimacy of the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just asked whether it was a legitimate decision, and that is not being denied. Right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what is strange about the fact that the Guards Brigade, whose commander is my aide-de-camp, should be subordinated to the military office of the president of the republic. And I assume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think the witness can speculate about this. This is General Perisic's letter. You can ask him to interpret it if he can, but this is going to be pure speculation on his part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. If so, then there was no need for him to comment upon the letter during the examination-in-chief either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can comment on it, but to ask him speculative questions isn't going to assist anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to that, in relation to General Perisic's allegation that officers were being appointed or rather generals were being appointed and promoted, apart from the general staff, I would like to ask you to take a look at the minutes from the fifth session of the Supreme Defence Council, so that was the 9th of June, 1998. This was just a month before his letter.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the opportunity of seeing these minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Point 2, personnel matters, the minutes. And I am quoting from the minutes: "General Perisic informed the participants in the session that the senior staff discussed this issue."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it all right now? Have you got this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here that what the chief of general staff said is approved, and so on and so forth. And it says that if the activities of the Albanian --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to read slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Read more slowly, would you. Read more slowly. The interpreters are asking. And where are you -- identify where you are reading from, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I am reading the minutes from the fifth session of the Supreme Defence Council, from the 17th of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, it's the 9th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, it's the 17th of June.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the meeting was held on the 9th. And it was just registered then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, that's right. But I'm just looking at the date on the document when it was entered into the records, but it's true that the session was actually held on the 9th of June, 1998. That's right.
