And this is where the chief of general staff spoke about the situation in Kosovo, and then on page 3, it says that "if terrorist activities escalate," so these are the conclusions that were adopted unanimously by the SDC, it says, number 2, "that if the terrorist activities of the Albanian separatist movement escalate, the Yugoslav army will intervene appropriately." So in relation to the instructions that you read out a moment ago, is it clear that there is full legality in terms of using the army there in order to combat terrorism in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If these instructions are based on this decision, then absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me now, item 2, personnel issues, it's on the same page, the text continues right after the conclusions related to item 1. It says: "General Perisic informed the persons attending the session that with regard to that issue - and this is in reference to personnel issues, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was the senior staff of the general staff that discussed this and it was approved by the Ministry of Defence according to the law of the Yugoslav army, and thereupon he made the following proposal to the Supreme Council of Defence. And then under number 1, it says: "On reaching a decision on the cessation of professional military service," and then it is mentioned according to the assessment of a medical military commission, then by force of law, and then according to the needs of the service and promotion to a higher rank in appropriate order, and then promotion to the rank of major general, and then regulating the situation, the service of general personnel, and then who was appointed where to command which particular unit and so on and so forth. There are several pages that go on. And ultimately, it says: "The Supreme Defence Council has fully adopted the proposal of the chief of general staff of the Yugoslav army, Colonel-General Momcilo Perisic on personnel issues in the army." So that is written on the minutes of the session of the 9th of June. And a month after that, Perisic writes in this letter of his that promotions take place without consulting the general staff. Do you know what this actually referred to? Because even in these minutes a month before that, it is obvious that there were consultations and all his proposals were unanimously accepted by the Supreme Defence Council. So what did these writings of his refer to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I read this letter that Mr. Perisic wrote to you in the month of July, precisely this item 5, that is to say, conducting personnel policies without legal basis and without criteria or decree, I imagine that this pertained to promotions and transfers. That is to say, without the general staff and the senior staff of the general staff knowing about this. Then also what it says here in the minutes from the session of the SDC held on the 9th of June, 1998, this is not binding upon the SDC. During the four years of my term of office, practically the senior staff of the chief of general staff made proposals, and the assumption was that they knew best what the quality of the generals was, and I see that it was done in this case, too. And the Ministry was consulted as far as I can see according to the names of the persons, the generals who are retired. These were generals who were in the Ministry of Defence, and I imagine that's why the Ministry was consulted. And the conclusion itself shows that the Supreme Defence Council accepted all the proposals of the chief of general staff. So I believe that this paper is self-explanatory, at least the one from the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there is no denying that all of this went through the general staff. Was anybody promoted without the knowledge of the chief of general staff, or the general staff as such?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my term of office, no one was. I don't know about your term. But even Article 136 of the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia provides for this possibility. Only to notify the chief of general staff that the president has the right to -- this kind of promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's a good thing for him to be notified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he certainly was notified. But he points out here that he has some right that is not based on the constitution or the law on the army that this has to be his proposal. That would practically mean that he were usurping the right that is only vested in the president of the FRY. Is that right or not right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is only the right of the president of the FRY to promote generals and appoint them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That will do. Thank you, Mr. Lilic. And then it says "material allocations outside the framework of regulations." Now, I would like to remind you of what you said. Materiel resources. You said during your testimony that this was done through the Ministry of the Interior according to a decision reached by the government of the FRY. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, he says: "You frequently order me to provide immoveable and moveable property for the needs of the MUP." Since you were in Kosovo at the time as well, and since you were very well informed by the -- about the entire situation, I assume that you will remember that there were many ambushes that were organised by Albanian terrorists. They shot at police vehicles, they killed policemen who were moving along roads in order to change shifts at checkpoints or people who were simply patrolling roads in regular police vehicles. Do you recall that there was casualties, there were deaths of policemen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the communication routes were in a way under the control of terrorists from Kosovo and Metohija and that police checkpoints were often exposed to their attacks. And also, the fact that I travelled to Kosovo and Metohija was highly risky. We had to use different means of transportation therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, since you were the person who commanded the army in war and peace over four years of time, and then as Deputy Prime Minister, you were there and you testified about these attacks against the police, was it logical for the army to make available a few APCs to the police so that they could safely communicate when they were going to change shifts? They were not supposed to be sitting pigeons that would be killed by Albanian terrorists and ambushed by them.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just correct you. There was no need for me to command the army during a war. I was not its commander in chief in war. As for the status of president in peacetime, that is clearly defined. But this was an explanation. As for whether it was necessary to give a few carriers or several, I believe that it was not only necessary but it was absolutely indispensable to protect the lives of these people who were exposed to terrorist attacks every day. But of course, this could have been regulated through all the necessary documentation. And I don't believe that anybody is denying that, that it should be transferred to the police in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not a question of transferring resources; this was simply in order to protect the lives of policemen who were unprotected in Kosovo. And therefore, it was logical to make available to them some of these technical resources that the army did not really need. The army, therefore, did not remain without the technical equipment they needed; on the other hand, the lives of policemen were protected. Isn't that logical?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think that the lives of these men were supposed to be protected, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. And then it says "immovable property." No immovable property was given to the police. It was simply requested in order to economise, if I can put it that way. Some groups of special police units were supposed to be staying at military barracks so that they would not have to have special people who would be guarding them, having some of their members stand guard. Over there, they could stay and they could get their meals, et cetera, and then go on carrying out their regular assignments. So that is nothing -- it's not that anything was done without regard to regulations. And couldn't General Perisic take care of this with the government and the Ministry without any problem? Would anybody have raised the issue?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the duty of the Ministry of Defence, and it is quite certain that everything you said is not being contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that is a misplaced, totally misplaced commentary, prompted merely by an effort to stretch certain arguments to the extreme, especially skipping over the lines of command for members of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For instance, when certain levels of command are being skipped over, do you believe that if an army commander asked to be received by the president of the republic to brief him on the situation in his jurisdiction, that the president of the republic may not do so if that man addresses the military office of the president which is also headed by a colonel-general, the same rank as General Perisic? Should the president of the republic ask General Perisic whether he be allowed to receive him or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which general you're referring to, but it isn't important. It's just an infringement of the singleness of command, and certainly the president of the republic doesn't have to ask. But respecting that principle of subordination, General Perisic should have been informed. He need not have been present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the fact that he is objecting that I was receiving someone means that he was informed. If he hadn't been informed, he couldn't object to it. Is that clear, Mr. Lilic, or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on that, Mr. Milosevic. I mean, this conclusion of yours is something I cannot comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I don't think that the rest of the letter deserves any further comment. In fact, the letter as a whole is a waste of time, considering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's pure comment, a matter for us to consider. If you've got any questions, ask them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to find just now, the decision on the formation of the staff. I think you have it, and you know what I'm referring to. You said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's find it. Just, let's find it so the witness has got the copy. The decision on the formation of the staff, do we have it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two decisions, if you're referring to the staff for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two decisions. I don't know which one you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Both decisions, as I wanted to clear up one particular point only. You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We're going to find it, first of all. Are these documents which the accused introduced?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're simply not sure, in the way it's described in the moment. It's not in the binder, otherwise the accused no doubt would have told us that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, if I may be of assistance, these are two documents, one I assume was signed by Mr. Djordjevic, police general, in mid-May. And another by the Minister of the Police, Mr. Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think those are the two documents you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see if we can find them. There's certainly a decision in tab 25, to establish a ministerial staff. That's dated the 16th of June. And there are two others that I recollect, but I don't know that I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but the document at tab 25... Yes, that's probably one of them. And that one is signed by Stojiljkovic, yes. We start off with tab 25, and we'll try and track the other one down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness have the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other one - Ms. Anoya very helpfully identified it - is 319, tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will be very brief in my questions regarding these documents. On the basis of your own direct insight, you stated that there were objections to the effect that the work of the security organs, public and state security, were not coordinated fully in Kosovo and Metohija, which Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 22827 to 22834. is always quite possible, of course. I'm not doubting such a conclusion. But is it quite clear that this solution to find ministerial staff in Pristina, signed by Colonel-General Vlastimir Stojiljkovic, assistant minister and head of the public security service, and the solution to form a staff, signed by the Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic, are documents whereby this problem was intended to be overcome, the problem of the lack of sufficient coordination. Is that right, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that with respect to the document signed by Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic. As for the previous one, as far as I know, at least, at direct briefings on the ground, it related only, I think, to the public security service. When I said that the coordination was not sufficient, it is not an assumption of mine. It was the conclusion reached at that information meeting in Djakovica where state security organs, or to be more precise Mr. Jovica Stanisic as head of that service, reported on the need to form such a unified staff with a unity of command because on the previous day, because of lack of synchronisation, during a clash with the terrorists, several people from the state security, if I recollect well, were killed. So this is the result of the information that I received and that I had with you, and the meetings with Milan Milutinovic. I think this staff was intended to overcome this lack of coordination. And I see by the list of names in the decision signed by Minister Stojiljkovic, that this was a mixed body of members from the state and public security headed by Major-General Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So a unified staff was formed by the Ministry of Internal Affairs, consisting of people from both the Public and the State Security Services, and even including heads of internal affairs secretariats in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. So this was a unification of the activities of the police through this staff that was formed by his decision by the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. I see that the commanders of special units were there; one that was within the State Security Service and another one that was within the public security department. So everything that existed on the ground from both departments were unified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this a move made in accordance with the suggestions and assessments that you yourself had made?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This staff was formed after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the date?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 16th of June, and the meeting with Milutinovic was held on the 13th of June. As far as I know after that big meeting in terms of the number of participants, another smaller meeting was held, and I think that was when the composition of this staff was decided on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that after that visit for which I gave my approval and expressed the necessity to make it, after hearing the information and comments and the meetings that you had on the 13th, as early as the 16th, this staff was formed and problems overcome that were highlighted at the time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you informed about all this at a meeting of the staff coordinated by Milutinovic. Wasn't that his job, being the president of Serbia and Kosovo being a part of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be even more specific than you. I think that that should have been his most important task at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any event, that is what was done, and there were no disagreements with respect to your assessments and the solution that was subsequently adopted. You said that efforts were made to revive economic activities, and that this task was assigned to Dusko Matkovic who was general manager of Sartid, the Smederevo ironworks which had some units even outside Smederevo. Do you know that certain efforts were invested that resulted in the revival of economic activities in some companies in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was convinced that we would not solve the problem in Kosovo and Metohija, but we could at least activate some potentials which would demonstrate Serbia's interest in the overall development of that part of the country as well. And I think that Dusko Matkovic was a perfectly qualified person for doing that. I think it's a good thing that the initiative was taken. Unfortunately, the results were not such to contribute to full stabilisation of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to what you mentioned on page 9 of your statement, when you say that Milutinovic headed this working group dealing with the crisis in Kosovo, and you say that that should have been his main task, which obviously it was at that time, you explain that senior representatives of Albanian and Serb communities should have cooperated. But that your proposals did not meet with understanding as far as I gather from your statement. Perhaps this is some kind of misunderstanding because I assume you know full well how many times a delegation of the government of Serbia went for meetings in Kosovo to meet with a delegation of the Kosovo Albanians. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no dispute regarding the activities of the government of Serbia and the delegations led by Mr. Ratko Markovic, I believe, who was vice-premier at the time. And the quotation that you refer to relates to direct contacts with Albanians who were not in the top leadership or high-level representatives of Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija. It relates to the actual inhabitants of the crisis areas, and I think that you remember that there were some such meetings in the area of Batusa, Junicko Polje. And even General Samardzic had concrete discussions with several families who accepted the protection of the army of Yugoslavia. Unfortunately, this was not developed any further, and I don't know what happened afterwards. I was not involved in those activities in Kosovo and Metohija. I think a dozen of them came to the barracks in Djakovica asking for the protection of the army of Yugoslavia. They were given that protection and were taken by military buses back to their homes. After that, I lost all touch, so I don't know why this method of communicating with the population was interrupted because I'm convinced that dialogues with prominent Albanians and Serbs were just as necessary as those at the level of the top leadership of the Republic of Serbia and the Kosovo Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I quoted to you yesterday what I said at a meeting of the main board of the party when I insisted on this dialogue. Emphasising that it was not reserved only for government representatives and leaders of Albanian political parties but that it should be conducted at all levels from the level of villages, local communes, towns, formal and informal occasions, and every other occasions so as to reduce tensions and to achieve understanding. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this connection, that is, the coming of Albanians seeking protection, is it clear that they were seeking protection in order to be safe from Albanian terrorists and other groups? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so, but as far as my competence is allowed, I did make an appeal to General Samardzic as well that they should equally protect them from Albanian extremists, but also from Serb extremists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was, in fact, their assignment. Yesterday, we discussed this, and the position of the leadership was that all citizens had to be protected, and that every perpetrator of any crime had to be arrested and handed over to the judiciary. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wish to save time. You mentioned some training centres, and a decision was produced here. Is it true that the state leadership, our state leadership, was opposed to any training centres being organised, especially not for people who were not citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume you're moving from Kosovo and Metohija now to the situation in Bosnia, if I'm not mistaken. If you're referring to the centre from 1995 that I refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether that is correct. I didn't wish to leave out that question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a general position taken by the leadership, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear on one point, an explanation you gave, in fact. And it's on page 16 of the shorter statement that you gave, that during the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that two different Territorial Defences existed, one legal one, pursuant to the constitution, the other one set up and composed of volunteers. Whose Territorial Defence do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps this wasn't quite the right translation of it because the first statement was not authorised. I assume that I did authorise the second one. But when we speak of the principle of Territorial Defence, then it was pursuant to the constitution of the state at the time, the legitimate armed force which, under given conditions, acted together with the JNA. And these sorts of Territorial Defences were republican, and they later formed the armies of the former Yugoslav republics. And to use the term that is used here, unlawful or illegal, this refers to volunteer units who were based on the principle of homeland units, and the area in which its members lived. If that's what you mean, the volunteer units made up of men from different parts of the regions, the home guard sort of system, so not the complex organisation that these generally imply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, as we're talking about these units, is it common knowledge that, for the most part, the volunteer units of some paramilitary formations were set up by some political parties, in fact? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I mentioned that in the course of my testimony during these two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Socialist Party of Serbia, did it ever set up any paramilitary formation at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. That went against the grain of our programme provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to Kosovo for a moment. Do you know that all the officers had detailed knowledge of international law?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of international war law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the duty of all officers, not only in Kosovo and Metohija but in any other unit too, in any other part of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And there was even an order issued during the aggression in Kosovo in 1999 according to which all the soldiers had copies of the Geneva Conventions on them.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and as far as I know, they did have copies of the Geneva Conventions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that an army acts according to orders, and the police are given -- also issued orders to catch criminals, if somebody heard of a crime being committed, were they duty-bound to apprehend the perpetrators and file a criminal report with the court authorities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was their professional duty, and their duties as human beings. And I don't think anybody abused those.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: On condition that they did not abuse those authorisations, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, to go back to your letter, I'm not going to dwell on it for any length of time.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which letter are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The letter to me concerning the talks. You said they met Kohl and so on. And then we come to the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have a copy, if he doesn't already. Remind us of the tab number. We have had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 27 and 28, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are the 5th of May and the 17th of May, 1999. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, looking through this letter, and I should like to focus on page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which one is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is a quotation which reads as follows: "The law --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which letter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the letter of the 5th of May, addressed to me by Mr. Lilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Tab 27, yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Actually, on page 1, you say that the essence of the talks and the possible initiative on our part consists in the following: "All activities must be directed towards the United Nations," et cetera. The principles on which a decision in our favour may be reached, the return of refugees, guarantees from the FRY, the OSCE, and the UN, and so on and so forth. Now, you say on page 2, in the middle of the page 2, that is why after detailed talks with Dr. Helmut Kohl, the former chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany, and talks with Dr. R. Vranitsky, the former chancellor of Austria, the most rational solution is as follows... That's right, isn't it? That's what you say?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it was Dr. F. Vranitsky, that was his initial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Accept a UN mission. That comes under -- well, it's not under a number of any kind but it comes first, that's the first point. And then it says as well as the presence of Russia, proposed the presence of one more permanent member, England or France from Europe, which will, as you say, attract the approval of the USA because this is a guarantee from my interlocutors and with China create the conditions for the adoption of such a resolution. And then you go on to state: My personal opinion is that it is necessary to propose Italy, Greece, Poland, Slovakia, Belorussia, the Ukraine, and especially Austria as a neutral country, and of course, the presence of countries that are friendly towards us, and you mention Libya as a case in point. And then you go on to say what the FRY would obtain from all this, would gain from it all, in fact. Everything that you put forward in this letter of yours which emerges from the discussions you had with Kohl refers exclusively to this brief quotation in the middle of page 2, that is to say, to accept a UN mission, and as well as the presence of Russia, to propose two other permanent members of the UN Security Council to create the necessary conditions. And then you present your own personal views about that and say what would be gained by behaving in that way. So the entire proposal is -- consists, in fact, of this basic point: The acceptance of a UN mission and who was supposed to be in it. Is that right, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right, then. Explain to me what else this says because the latter part of your letter goes on to explain what we would gain, and you say accept a UN mission and who should be present. So what else is there, in your view, which was Kohl's proposal, the gist of Kohl's proposal?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That so on condition had the two of us not had a conversation two days prior to that where I told you in great detail, and if you want me to, I'll repeat what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We don't need to hear that again, we have the letter before us, and the letter states to accept a UN mission, accepting a UN mission. That is what it says in your letter. Now, I'm asking you this --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I continue my answer, if I may. I'll try and explain to you what I mean, if you will allow me to do so. The first and most important principle was why the talks were held at all. The talks were held because the NATO bombing lasted much longer than Belgrade thought it would go on for. And it was my idea to try and make use of something that was possible at the time. And so several meetings were held, and this is just one segment from a meeting dated the 3rd of May from Bonn, and I don't want to elaborate upon that meeting because you know the details of that meeting very well. But all we had to do was to respond and it was to stop the bombing, stop the air strikes, and what would happen after the air strikes had stopped. So you extracted this from the contents of the first page. And then it goes on to state what would happen after the bombing, after the air strikes, the activities ranging from a political agreement with the Albanians, the conference in Vienna, the withdrawal of the JNA and special MUP units at the level before the NATO pact aggression. And I'm sure you'll remember the meeting at the end of October at your office with Mr. Solana and Mr. Holbrooke present, and I received information as to what was proposed. If you would like me to do so, I will be happy to repeat it but I don't think there's any need for me to do that. And then there were talks to revive the microstructure after the NATO aggression, the FRY's integration into the international and European courses, and specific international institutions. And then afterwards, if we act upon these modalities and solutions, it says what I think we would gain. So the last four points are what I think would be gained. And I think today, from this distance of time, I am far more convinced of this, in fact, that we should have attempted to do so. Of course, you could have had different information yourself, information and intelligence I didn't know about. But we should have acted along those lines because it was in everybody's interest to have the NATO bombing stopped. Of course, we had the greatest interest in doing so with all the casualties and destruction this caused, but I don't have to tell you of other people's interest of those who were included in this project. I don't want to mention their names, but if we want to open that chapter of the book, we can do so. I think that this was a very good opportunity to attempt to stop the bombings. And in Mr. Kohl's conviction, this was very possible. And several days afterwards, the G7 plus one, or G8, meeting was held in Berlin where it was possible to hold negotiations of this type, and if I can say in invert the commas, as a service to our side, all that was required was that you should accept this because you were the person that made the decisions as president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And it was up to you to state publicly that you accept this or give an initiative for this plan to go forward. And I considered at that time and still consider this today that it wouldn't have cost you anything to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course it didn't cost anything to discuss these issues, but we didn't need so many words, and we don't need so many words because this proposal was -- in fact, boiled down to this: To accept the UN mission. That is the crux and substance of the proposal. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The substance of the proposal was a condition for everything that I go on to enumerate. And the condition -- there were two things; first of all, to accept a UN mission, and secondly, in view of the generally accepted position, your position first and foremost that was generally accepted in our country, that we could not accept NATO pact troops at any cost. And the second point was a modality, ways and means to resolve and implement this decision, and it is stated that this was a component part for the condition of everything that was to follow. So we had to have a majority in the permanent UN -- of the permanent UN Security Council members. And I don't want to mention names but we would not accept the USA at the time, Great Britain either, but France was possible and logical. So that is the third member, along with China and Russia, although you did have promises from Russia that it would voice its veto, although I don't think they ever fulfilled that promise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, not to waste more time, because my time is very limited. Do you happen to remember telling me that I should write with my own hand, in my own hand and state that this kind of solution should be accepted, that is to say, acceptance of a UN mission for our part. Is that right, that is what Kohl asked of you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that you ought to make a public offer via the information media to that effect, and you wrote to me, and I still have that piece of paper. I hold it very dear for everything else that happened in the negative sense, of course, that's what I mean. And it says there that you should reply with useful unclarity, a lack of clarity, and I knew what that meant, ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have a concrete question, because the letter was made public. Everybody can read it. And the proposal was to accept the UN mission. And in my own hand, I did write this piece of paper, I haven't got it, you've got it. You took it. But I do have a copy from this book. It is called "Water and Flood" -- "Water and Fire." And the book publishes this text of the piece of paper that I wrote. Can we place that on the ELMO, from the "Fire and Flood" book, there is something written in my hand there and your hand. And everyone can read it if it is put on the overhead projector. Put it on the ELMO, and then I think that you'll agree that what I wrote there is what I indeed did write. I haven't got an extra copy, but I can read my own handwriting. And I see that you have framed it, framed this portion. What I wrote was: "The UN mission. We will accept the UN mission and we are ready and prepared to discuss all aspects of the mission and negotiate about it (The term of office, structure, duration, and et cetera, and all other questions)." So this was in response to your own letter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be placed on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can see this written out in my own handwriting. There is no handy ambiguity in any of that. It states clearly that we shall accept the UN mission and are ready to negotiate as to the details. And one and all can read this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you answer the question, could you first of all identify the document and state whether it is an authentic document or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the lower corner, there's a comment by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which was, since it's not in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Does not accept a proposal for a possible plan and puts forward an idea," and in inverted commas, "useful ambiguity." I can send you this piece of paper. I don't think it's vital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is completely irrelevant. THE ACCUSED [Interpretation] Let's see my handwriting put on the ELMO, please. So that people can see my handwriting, what I wrote up at the top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said that that is quite correct. There is nothing that is disputed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, I'm not saying this for your benefit, but I'd like to it to be placed on the ELMO, on the overhead projector so that others can see what I wrote in my own handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Doesn't matter. We're not wasting time with your displaying documents. The Court has seen the document. It's not for anybody else. What is it you want the witness to deal with? He has agreed that it's authentic. I'll also note that it has been exhibited already as part of Exhibit 152. And it pertains to the book and the appendices from it. What do you want the witness to answer about this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted it to be placed on the overhead projector for us, Mr. May, to be able to comment on it together so we have this all of us together on the overhead projector. And I don't see why that is not possible for us to comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got it now. Now, what is the question you want to ask about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, does it state loud and clear there in my own handwriting, and I'm reading here from the screen: "We are going to accept the UN mission and we are ready to discuss all aspects of the mission (mandate, structure, duration and other issues)." So that's what it says there in my own handwriting. So tell me, please, what ambiguity is there, or what lack of clarity is there there? Because in your letter it says, "accept a UN mission," and my response says, "we are going to accept the UN mission." We are now ready to discuss all the details, mandate, structure, duration, and other issues.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, please go ahead. That's why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my letter, it says "accept UN mission" without any reservations, that's number one. And number two is accept one of the NATO members, one of the permanent members of the Security Council of the UN. And this is what you gave me as a possible answer to Mr. Kohl. And I said that this kind of answer will not be accepted. And the -- it was explicitly said that you should make a statement through the media that these two positions are being accepted. And then everything would have happened as it should have happened. Of course, there were journalists of some international TV stations that were engaged. I don't know, until the present day. And if ever I manage to find out, I will appreciate it, why were they expelled from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know either.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they worked in our interest as a matter of fact. And then I asked you, at the personal request of Mr. Kohl, to have the journalist of one of the German agencies released. He was arrested and he was in our prison. And you accepted that, but this was done regrettably ten or 15 days later, after Zivadin Jovanovic and the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Germany met. So this was portrayed in a completely different way. This letter is preceded by some other things as well. My letter is yet another attempt for you to look at things that we discussed, not through letters but in a personal meeting and for a long time. And again, I'm referring to my meeting with Mr. Vranitsky before that. And then a meeting with the leader of the Libyan Jamahiriya, Mr. Ghadhafi. It was devoted to the same topic. And as a matter of fact, if I can put it mildly, we were very unfair towards him who asked to talk to Mr. Rugova, but he was told that he would have to be in Pristina so he could go to Italy the same day. Perhaps this didn't have anything to do with you but some people did not have the right feeling for what we needed at that point in time. And I don't think anything was more important or urgent at that point than the cessation of bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Probably there's not a single citizen of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia who wouldn't share that opinion that nothing was more urgent than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the usher come back, instead of having to stand there. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if I can clarify this further, if you wish to, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a minute, for the Court you can clarify it. It's not just a matter of answering him. It's to the Court you're giving evidence. Mr. Lilic, you clarify it, clarify the position so we can understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a simple letter at all and presented in such simple terms, it may look as a matter of circumstances, something that will be used against President Milosevic then specifically. That was not my ambition. This was simply a wish to make an effort to start talks with Mr. Kohl. And that this is correct is proved by the meeting. After that, I could not see you. I could not reach you by telephone. I could not get in touch with you at all for days, for about 13 days, I believe. I can't even remember exactly any more. On the 17th of May, a meeting was held and it was only dedicated to this letter. It was at the Presidency of Serbia, and it was chaired by the then president of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, you explained that during the examination-in-chief. Why are we using time now for you to explain it yet again. If you have something to add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't you criticise him for wasting time. Most of it's taken up with you. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Page 23 of your shorter statement, you say yourself "after meeting with Helmut Kohl in May 1999, conveyed his proposal," and you say that my reaction was a positive one. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was your first impression, that's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I wrote that we accept UN presence. And what was given as a thought as to who would take part in this, well, isn't that a question that should be negotiated? The status, structure, and so on, the mandate, and everything else. Isn't that customary? So the proposal for the UN presence to be accepted was approved, and the structure, the mandate, and everything else are questions that have to be negotiated. Isn't that something that is a plain fact?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not being contested, but the strategic point of that talk was not accepted, and I could not accept it because you didn't want to authorise me to discuss that subject, although I had asked for that. The strategic point of accepting some of the NATO members who are UN Security Council permanent members, they should be accepted, too. Those who did not take part in the campaign or aggression against Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that that is part of my answer, too, that we are prepared to discuss the structure. So it implies that the approach to the entire proposal is a positive one, but that we are prepared to discuss the structure.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, but I do have to respond to this statement you just made. We did not have the right to negotiate the structure, and this right was not exercised later on when this was accepted by way of ultimatum, that this kind of plan would be carried through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We are going to return to this ultimatum plan of Ahtisaari and Chernomyrdin as you had put it, but the explanation that you gave and that is in this book, as well, which was made on the basis of your statements, Kohl explained that he could exercise influence over Yeltsin because he had given his regime hundreds of -- thousands of billions of deutschmark. Do you know that Russia was the only member of the Security Council that quite openly made efforts to help stop the bombing, that Yevgeny Primakov came to Belgrade, and then after that, Chernomyrdin came, so both Primakov and Chernomyrdin, depending on the role that was entrusted to them by then President Yeltsin, and that Russia quite simply was the only member of the Security Council that publicly and openly made efforts to have the bombing stopped and to find some kind of a compromise solution.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect to Mr. Primakov and Mr. Chernomyrdin, their help was really more than marginal, according to what I know. And you probably know that even better. Mr. Chernomyrdin directly took part in the preparation of the Ahtisaari plan, and later on, this is my conviction, it was signed after 37 days of incessant bombing from this point in time. Of course, I didn't have to be aware of all the negotiations that were going on, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were things that were going on and this was, at any rate, in our interest. But now that we are talking about Ahtisaari and Chernomyrdin, isn't this plan actually contained in Resolution 1244 of the Security Council of the UN?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is contained in Resolution 1244. I'm not talking about its legitimacy, of course. It was signed, and the Kumanovo agreement was signed on military matters, and it is very reminiscent of the Rambouillet plan. And it caused great, great harm to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Of course, this is just my opinion, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, we all wanted the war to end. We all cared about that. Do you remember well what is written in the Ahtisaari-Chernomyrdin plan and in Resolution 1244? What is written there is that the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia are guaranteed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have to interrupt. An assertion there that in the light of the witness's earlier evidence I would like him to clarify. It's put to you "we all wanted the war to end." Was that the true situation at the time or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, Mr. May, that everybody in Yugoslavia could hardly wait for the war to end. But it is my conviction that it could have ended earlier than it actually did. So that is the only difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You referred earlier to people who wanted to break NATO or used some expression such as that. At what time were those sort of sentiments being expressed? At this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke about such feelings among some of the activists of the Yugoslav Left who said that NATO's backbone would break in the case of Yugoslavia. Perhaps somebody really did think along these lines, that a new world would be established, a different kind. I don't think these were very reasonable ideas but that was talked about in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think there was a single citizen of Yugoslavia who did not want the war to end as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said Mr. Milosevic that I am convinced that everybody wanted it to end as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now, when this unofficial communication of yours was favourably received, and it was said and written in my hand "we accept this" --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you for a second. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead. Interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last question was gone on for a long time, and then I lose sight of some of the things that you have been saying. So this was not an unofficial communication. It was very official, with your blessing, with your approval. And going out of the country several times, under bombs, during the bombing, cannot be unofficial. This was done with the knowledge of the Minister of Foreign Affairs, and he refused to allow the ambassador to be present with me because he said there was no need, and afterwards he said that he did not remember that. So it could not be an unofficial meeting with Mr. Kohl or with any other officials with whom I had intensive talks over those several weeks. And you know that talks to foreign dignitaries at very high level started even before the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, I did not want to diminish the fact that you left with my approval, that you went with my approval, and with my knowledge. And from that point of view, certainly, in an official capacity. But when I say "unofficial," I mean that Kohl at that time was no longer in an official office. He was an influential person, but he was not the chancellor of Germany, who we were negotiating with. However, a former chancellor of Germany who could exercise his personal influence, but not the office of chancellor, which he no longer held. So in that sense, I said unofficial. And now, whether during the official office held by Mr. Kohl, Germany actively took part in the breakup of Yugoslavia, that's a question that I'm putting now.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not being challenged, their influence. May I finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not being contested, the frequent visits of Mr. Genscher and their influence over what happened in Slovenia and in Croatia if you wish. But I thought personally that this was -- this was even more of a reason for Mr. Kohl to be the right kind of interlocutor, primarily bearing in mind the facts that you just referred to. At that time, Germany was divided. There are a lot of protests, and that I think Mr. Fischer's government was already -- Mr. Genscher's government was already facing a great deal of problems, and also Mr. Fischer who was heading the Green Party at the time. And it is precisely for all these reasons that he was a good person to talk to at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was a good person to talk at the time no doubt, and there was this wish to talk to everyone, especially those who could be good interlocutors and that was an expression of our efforts to avail ourselves of every opportunity to stop the war.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in view of his unofficial position, do you think that the unofficial position of Helmut Kohl could carry more weight? He did not really show much friendship towards Serbia, especially not at the time of the breakup of Yugoslavia, or in terms of the official initiative and efforts made by Russia and their official representatives to help stop the bombing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should be aware of what I'm going to say by way of an answer. I think that the overall reputation enjoyed by Mr. Kohl, and I'm talking about that time and his preparations for a comeback on the political scene of Germany and also his campaign for the European parliament gave him such great importance that I'm quite certain from this distance that we had a good chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's precisely this chance that we wanted to use, and that is why we favourably responded to his proposal.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not favourably respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we just showed my very own handwriting a few minutes ago, and I say that we accept the presence of the UN. On page 23, in the shorter statement, you say that I did not refuse you a single time, that I supported you all the time, that I said that he should be given a decent answer, that a favourable answer should be given and so on. And of course, to spell this out very specifically, the mandate of the mission, the structure of the mission, and so on. Is that right, is that what you wrote?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the way things went during the first day we met, Mr. Milosevic. The second day, we did not send an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not say that an answer should not be sent. I meant that this answer, because you insisted upon my own handwriting, and you insisted that I write this in my own hand, and you said that this would be sent to Kohl.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't really think that I wanted to fax this handwriting to Mr. Kohl. I believe that this dialogue of ours is pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think it's pointless, too.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, and I claim that you should have spoken out in favour of accepting these two minor conditions, as you put it, so that we would get to the big issue on page 3. And after that, Mr. Kohl travelled to the United States, but I think it would really be impolite of me to speak here about all the things that were discussed with Mr. Kohl then because he's not being discussed here now. Quite simply an attempt was being made to stop the bombing already in the beginning of May 1999. Why? I never got that answer. But I did get quite an answer as concerns myself personally, and all the things that happened to me, but I don't wish to speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing happened to you from my side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt now so the witness can clarify. We've seen this document in the accused's handwriting. What happened then, after that document was written?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That document was written as soon as I got back, so I think this was on the 4th, and my comment was written on the 5th. President Milosevic was supposed to appear in public before our media and say that he accepts a UN mission and that he agrees that among them, there should be some of the members of NATO, and this was defined in the second line here where it says that "one of the three permanent members of the Security Council should be accepted, either the USA or Great Britain or France."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I did not get this kind of response from Mr. Milosevic, I did not send an answer to Mr. Kohl, that the facts I'm presenting are correct is testified to by our activity after the end of the bottoming when you asked to have contacts and communication with these people re-established, that I should do that. And then it was far more difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's 12.15, time to adjourn. We can continue with this afterwards. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, you had a talk about this letter of yours with the most responsible leaders of Yugoslavia. Is that right? Of Yugoslavia and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 17th of May in the Presidency of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. The Presidency of Serbia. Who were the people who were present on that occasion? By name and position they held.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chairman, who was to chair the meeting, was Mr. Milan Milutinovic, who was at the time president of the Republic of Serbia. Then there was Gorica Gajevic, on his left, if I remember well, who was the Secretary-General of the Socialist Party of Serbia; Miomir Minic, a senior SPS official, and I think he was at the time president of the Chamber of Citizens in the Assembly; Zivadin Jovanovic, the official Minister of Foreign Affairs; Mirko Marjanovic, who was at the time president of the Assembly of Republic of Serbia -- no, sorry, president of the government, Prime Minister. And Dragan Tomic, president of the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the president of the Republic of Serbia, the Prime Minister of the Republic of Serbia, the president of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, the president of the Federal Assembly, or rather, of the Chamber of Citizens of the Federal Assembly, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Yugoslavia, and the Secretary-General of the party. Do you consider, in view of the significance for the country, for the people, for all of us, when such a cardinal question was being discussed at the height of the war, that is, the possibility of an initiative to accept the presence of the United Nations, which I had already accepted and given you a note to that effect, that such a subject needed to be reviewed and examined by the most responsible representatives of the authorities who were, furthermore, in the top leadership of the Socialist Party of Serbia, as you were as well at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, will you please not repeat saying that you had agreed to what I suggested after the preliminary talk with Mr. Kohl. And here's another reason in support of that: In a letter of the 30th, which is not contained in this binder, addressed to you personally when I present to you a plan indicating certain names that I do not wish to mention now, and at the bottom of the letter, it says, it is implied that you should take a decision to appoint me as a special envoy to establish the principles with representatives of the international community for the establishment of peace in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, a special envoy as a former president. Among the first questions that Mr. Kohl asked me was whether I had the authority to agree on anything, so it wasn't sufficient for you just to put on a piece of paper that you agreed to a discussion regarding the mandate of the UN forces. What -- as I explained a moment ago, as regards the meeting of the 17th of May, it was everything but certainly not a meeting discussing the contents of the letter as it was my personal letter addressed to you. And it was addressed out of the best of intentions, and not for any other reasons, as some of your associates may have thought. And if you wish, I can repeat what they said. This meeting, to my astonishment, revealed that all of them had a copy of the letter I had sent to you -- I apologise to the interpreters -- and it was used -- simply I must use a rather nasty word, a meeting at which I was exposed to terrible criticism. I think that was not the time and place, at the height of the bombing campaign, to discuss my intentions behind my writing that letter to you and any responsibility that I may have for that. I don't wish to reveal the extent to which they were not informed about the matters they discussed. So the meeting on the 17th had nothing to do with consultations about such a serious issue as the one we discussed. And I must add that Mr. Milutinovic was informed about all those talks before the meeting, as was Mr. Zivadin Jovanovic, who forgot about that at this meeting, because he forgot that I went to see him the day before I left on my trip, in agreement with you, and asked for Mr. Jeremic to accompany me, because he had been an ambassador to Germany and he spoke German, which I do not. And I also asked to be briefed as far as possible and provided with information about talks that you and Mr. Chernomyrdin had had. Mr. Jovanovic forgot about that, and his greatest criticism of me was for interfering in his affairs. So this was not a consultation, it was simply a party tribunal at a time and place that was inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the witness is referring to a letter that doesn't appear to be amongst our binders. It would be appropriate if the accused was given a copy of that letter for him to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know what paper -- I don't know what papers the witness has. They may be private papers. He could either be told to put them away, if that's what concerns you, or if he has no objection, they could be produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be appropriate for him to be asked that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As for this letter, I think we actually probably have a copy somewhere, and we can get it copied if the witness wants us to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we have the date of it, do we? Mr. Lilic, you've heard what I said. Is there any objection, any personal objection, to that letter being produced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a letter written just before all of these events, and it consists of a little plan that I presented Mr. Milosevic with. It contains names of people that I didn't wish to be made public. But of course, I have no objection for this letter to be shown. I hope that Mr. Milosevic has it. It's not one letter, it's three letters, including one that came from the Libyan embassy in Belgrade. But I really do not think that it is of relevance for all the things we're talking about, except if Mr. Milosevic insists on having it, I'll be glad to provide him with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not a question for you, it's a question for the Court whether it's relevant or not. Perhaps the Prosecution can look for it. Since the witness is going to have to come back at some stage to give his evidence, no doubt this can be part of documents which are disclosed. Rather than waste time further on it now, let us move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, just a second, if I may. I have that letter here with me. I can provide it immediately to be copied, so there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be the Prosecution have the originals, and also translations, so they could be shown it. Otherwise, it can be copied. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to see this, because I don't have any other documentation except for that that I have been provided with. I don't know what the witness has in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't now just off the cuff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me have it. Mr. Lilic, we have the document here. You've heard the accused ask for it. I gather you've no objection to his having a look at it. Are you concerned that he doesn't mention the names which are in here, or is he free to ask you any questions about it, as far as you're concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask you kindly that he not mention those names. Mr. Milosevic knows these people, and I think there is no need for him to refer to them specifically, unless you want us to go into closed session, and then we can go into far greater detail if Mr. Milosevic finds it necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, you can have these, have a look at these letters. You can ask questions about them, but if you want to go into any of the names that are there, you must go into private session. Are the Prosecution having a look for them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have an English version. We are getting it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, I am not going to put any questions related to the names of these persons. For the most part, this has to do with something that I wish to ask Mr. Lilic about. On the whole, this has to do with using informal ties that existed between Mr. Lilic and certain persons in order to establish contact with, perhaps, some significant factors that could speed up solutions. This name can be mentioned in open session, the most important person of this kind is former German chancellor Kohl.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lilic, let's go back to what we were discussing. This was a letter of yours that contains this proposal, and you claim that I did not give you an answer to that, although you have it in writing. This looked into many aspects, and you say that these people had the letter. Of course; I gave it to them, and I said, Please, sit down and have a meeting with Zoran Lilic, who had conducted these talks, and have consultations about this in order to assess the extent to which - how can I put this? - there are grounds for some kind of a belief that also in this way some progress can be made. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least according to the practice that existed in terms of our contacts and the coordination meetings you had that I did not attend, I think it was only natural that if what you said just now is correct, that this coordination meeting, this very small meeting, because Mr. Milutinovic did know about these activities, Mr. Zivadin Jovanovic knew about this, the others were not involved from any point of view in all of this in 1998, and also during all the months of the war. If it is correct, then it would only have been natural to have this meeting in your office. But their questions did not have to do with the essence of the letter itself; they had to do with why the letter had been written in the first place. As a matter of fact, some of them said that they had no idea what this was all about, but it should not have been written nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to go into --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for your agreement to this, I'm going to repeat for the fifth time that you did not give your agreement. It cannot be on a mere piece of paper. And it's not that I needed this consent; Mr. Kohl needed your personal consent, either by way of a public statement or in any other way that you should be quite aware of. I think that today we would have had a completely different situation; maybe it would have been different, maybe it would have been the same, I don't know, but on the basis of what I know concerning the proposal that was given to you towards the end of October by Mr. Solana in the presence of Mr. Holbrooke, all of this could have had a different dimension altogether. And the meeting you're referring to on the 17th of May, quite frankly, Mr. Milosevic, it had nothing to do whatsoever with consultations regarding to what I had written to you. It only had to do with the fact why I had written this to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go into a debate here in terms of what was discussed at the meeting that you had and that I did not attend. I just wanted to say that these were the top state officials. I just wanted to say that this was an issue of crucial importance and it was only natural that the top state leaders should be informed of this paramount question, and they received first-hand information from you since you took part in these communications. So that is something that I assume you're not denying, and I'm not denying it either.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd really be most pleased if the meeting evolved that way and according to that logic that you refer to just now and with that kind of intensity. But never mind, it had its consequences and today it doesn't really matter any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the very core of the matter. On the one hand, we had the official initiative of Russia, a public initiative, well-known to the entire world; on the other hand, we had an informal initiative. Does it stand to reason, is it logical that moving from a very formal communication and well-intentioned communication that Russia had, moving on to some informal communication would actually mean closing the door to the only official support at that time that we enjoyed, and it was from Russia? In terms of mediation and efforts made to obtain acceptable conditions for bringing the war to an end.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead. That's what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, and you can rest assured that it is quite correct and it can easily be proven correct, this is an initiative that was conveyed by Mr. Strobe Talbot to Mr. Ahtisaari, and Mr. Chernomyrdin only got into it later on at the proposal of Mr. Ahtisaari. And the most important thing is that it was not moving along parallel lines with the initiative that you call informal. It started after that. It was only after the 5th of May. My proposal to you was -- I mean, I'm really trying not to say anything here that would harm anyone who negotiated with you or who I talked to. These initiatives were supposed to evolve along parallel lines, and I think that's what the letter says. But of course, it was your right to go for the formal initiative, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this initiative, if we can call it that, the one you're referring to, was it perhaps a calculation that we lose even this one and only support we had at that point from a formal aspect, in terms of Russia's efforts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can interpret it that way nowadays because nothing was done even to try to talk about this other initiative and its substance. I don't see any good that would come out of the other initiative. According to the first proposal and the proposal that was given to you by Mr. Solana towards the end of October in Kosovo, according to your agreement with Holbrooke, there were supposed to be 12.000 troops, army troops, and 10.000 policemen. If the information given to me by my interlocutors is correct, Mr. Solana even offered logistic support by way of 10.000 army troops of NATO in order to disarm the KLA. Today, there is practically not a single soldier in Kosovo or a single policeman in Kosovo. As a matter of fact, there are less Serbs there than here in the prisons in the Hague. I'm one of those people, and I think that you know that full well, who wants to be proud of belonging to that people, and I want my son to be proud of the fact that he is a Serb. And I think that this is not useful for anyone. You know full well that my position regarding the military part of the agreement, the Kumanovo agreement is capitulation, and this is not a war that was won and it is not a agreement that was signed by somebody who had won the war, as there were some interpretations in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I really find it convenient that you said this, what you said just now. We really have to clarify these facts. Let's leave aside the letter now and the informal initiative which in my assessment and in the assessment of other officials --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been over this point and you've made it several times. There's no need to repeat it, whatever your view of this was. Now, if you're going on to another topic, go on to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to what you referred to just now, during the examination-in-chief, you mentioned General Marjanovic, who on behalf of Yugoslavia signed the Kumanovo agreement. I consider him to be a very able general, and a very honourable man. Do you know that in the Kumanovo agreement, there is no reference to NATO? It is the security forces of the international community that are referred to.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, Mr. Milosevic, how this particular noun, NATO, was left out. What you're saying is correct, but I think that you will also agree with me that today in Kosovo and Metohija, there are only NATO troops. There are no other forces of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is the greatest defeat and shame of the United Nations. The UN was used in order to do indescribable harm to our country after the NATO aggression. That's precisely what this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's stop there if you're making these sort of assertions. Mr. Lilic, you've heard what the accused has asserted. You can comment on it if you wish; if you agree with it, you may say so. It may not be of any assistance at all to this trial. But I'm not going to stop the accused from making it. Do you want to say anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say is that it is really terrible that at least that resolution, 1244, has not been implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is the whole point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
