utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope, Mr. May, you will not interrupt me. But to speed things up, since this is a document disclosed by Mr. Nice, it is my speech at the 4th congress of the Socialist Party of Serbia on the 17th of February, 2000, 02163379.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 7.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There will be an opportunity to use much of it, but before I move on to that, is it well known that the Resolution 1244 and the proposal of the G8 made by Chernomyrdin and Ahtisaari announcing at the airport already that they were bringing peace, and the whole of Yugoslavia expected peace finally to come, did it not envisage very strict terms for the stoppage of the war? Is it true, Mr. Lilic, that the most important was guarantees of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia by the United Nations? Is that right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the aggression on Yugoslavia was carried out without the permission of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a precedent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that precisely because NATO never managed to set foot on the soil of Yugoslavia, that our resistance pushed Clinton back to the UN to use the United Nations to make this agreement on the cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... points. The witness really can't give evidence for [Realtime transcript read in error "about"] Mr. Clinton. Now, let's move on. You want to ask about this speech.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do wish to ask the witness whether what I said at the time was true. But before I do that, in addition to guaranteeing the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the country without NATO managing to set foot on the soil of Yugoslavia, because we stopped it, that there were also guarantees that international forces would guarantee the security of all inhabitants in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate in those negotiations. I know what it is written, and the resolution we referred to implies that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at page 02163382, the fourth page of the speech. I would like to quote much more, but because of my restricted time, I will quote just a limited amount. And please comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, I want to correct the transcript. My intervention, ten or so lines up, what I said was the witness can't give evidence for Mr. Clinton, not about Mr. Clinton, as it says. It was for Mr. Clinton, that's the point. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope, Mr. May, that you will issue instructions to Mr. Clinton to come and testify when the time comes for that. And I do not think that this witness should testify for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So paragraph 4 from the top, I refer to the following: "The bombing of Serbia was ended by agreement between the Yugoslav state and representatives of the international community that representatives of the United Nations come to Kosovo with a view to establishing peace, order, and normal life for all those living there." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this written in the resolution? Was this stated in the Ahtisaari-Chernomyrdin agreement, coupled with guarantees for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the territory of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then I go on to say that "Serbia accepted the agreement with confidence, as well as the guarantees of the United Nations." So NATO, without the United Nations, committed aggression, and the United Nations acted in relation to Serbia, and Serbia accepted with trust the agreement and the guarantees of the United Nations. Is that right? Is that right, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what was stated, and that is what is written. You are familiar with my positions regarding that plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But then I go to say: "But nothing came of the peace." Because it says here "that they came to establish peace, a normal life for all those living there" but nothing came of the peace and still less of order, and no trace of normal life. "Albanian terrorism has been legalised and monitored by the United Nations representatives. Most Serbs have left Kosovo, and only a few remain there as living monuments reminding the world that it idly watches by the extermination of a people, a people which is at the present moment the most courageous in the world, despite a pile of statements, protests, outrage and disapproval coming from north and south, from east, and even from the west, the children of Kosovska Mitrovica have no guarantees for life. For the time being, their guarantees for life remain only their country and the people living in it." Mr. Lilic, is it true that despite these guarantees, that UN forces will protect all the citizens of Kosovo, introduce order, et cetera, that they have allowed several hundred thousand Albanians --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder what the relevance of all this is to this indictment. And the problem is that the time is very limited and if the accused simply uses opportunities here to repeat speeches for a different audience, it is wasting valuable time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The answer may be that you put the document in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that doesn't make the whole document admissible, and I put it in for a passage that comes earlier and tracks back to the relevant time with which we are concerned, and I'll come to that in re-examination. But this passage is of no relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the relevance for this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance is, Mr. May, the response of the witness that in spite of the guarantees of the United Nations, what happened happened. I'm now asking him what it is that happened and to what extent what happened was an abuse of the United Nations. So I'm asking the witness, is it true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But it's after the indictment period. It's after the period with which we are concerned. So the point is, is there any relevance as far as the indictment is concerned? I don't think there is. In any event, there are others who could deal with this if it does become relevant, I should have thought, besides this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. May; these are very substantive issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that these forces that came to Kosovo made it possible for several hundred thousand Albanians from Northern Albania to enter Kosovo without any control?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think you have to satisfy us as to what is it about the presence of NATO forces in Kosovo after the indictment period that makes it relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is relevant for the case, Mr. Robinson, because this conduct in fact proves the prolongation of the crime committed against the Serb people, against Serbia, against Yugoslavia, as a result of the NATO aggression during which I was indicted for alleged war crimes. Therefore, the presence -- you put it very well; the presence of the NATO forces, though they were not NATO forces literally, but forces of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Lilic, that the first forces that arrived in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, no. We haven't yet ruled on this. It's still not clear as to why you say the presence of those troops has anything to do with the indictment. What is the connection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The connection is the crime that the Clinton administration and NATO committed against Yugoslavia during the period when this so-called indictment was issued. And I wish the relevant facts linked to that to be established here. And I think the relevance of these questions cannot be challenged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, you've not established any relevance at all. Go on to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Lilic, do you remember that the first forces that arrived in Kosovo were Russian forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in the resolution, in addition to the matters that I have quoted, that is, guarantees for sovereignty, territorial integrity, and security for all, there was a provision regarding the return of a contingent of the army of the police of Yugoslavia to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, 1.500 military men, and I don't remember how many policemen, but that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So not one of those elements, that is, the guarantee of territorial integrity, guarantees of security, guarantees for the return of our contingent, were not respected because the rights of the United Nations were usurped by NATO.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That situation is quite evident. There is no return of our units there. There's no protection of borders on our part. The border crossings are absolutely out of control, so it is absolutely as you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've gone outside the ruling already. Now go back to something that's relevant. So anything during the war, certainly; during the conflict, certainly. But not after it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, during the war, many things happened that we have referred to. Unheard of crimes were committed against Serbs in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, Mr. Lilic, that under the auspices of the forces that were called the UN forces, tens of thousands of Serb houses have been burnt down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we're going to have to bring this to an end. We may have to bring your cross-examination to an end if you've got no more relevant questions. Do you understand that? Now, you heard the ruling: Nothing afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. If you do not allow me to put such questions to the witness, for the record, I wish to say that this prolongation of the war by the usurpation of the United Nations is the greatest disgrace for the UN --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to hear any speeches either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I say this because this illegal court is also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you want to have this matter adjourned now, you're going the right way about it, making speeches of this sort. Now, have you got any more relevant questions for this witness, in which case you can ask them; otherwise, we'll bring the examination to an end. You've got about a quarter of an hour more. And while I am dealing with matters, we'll exhibit the handwritten note about which there was so much evidence, in the accused's handwriting, the appendix to the book "Fire and Flood" with the next Exhibit number, D146. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, you occupied the top positions in Yugoslavia in the Socialist Party of Serbia, and you rank among the best-informed people - and those could be counted on the fingers of one hand - in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, informed on all events that took place. Do you have any information whatsoever about the fact that any organ whatsoever of the Republic of Serbia or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia organised or planned - I'm using words -- the words used in this false indictment, so it is relevant - whether you have any knowledge that any organ in an organised fashion or in a planned fashion committed any kind of crime, or ordered, or you can use whichever word you like here, from any aspect? Do you have any knowledge to that effect at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in the statement that I gave, you said that I never heard or was present when anybody issued an order or planned any kind of crime from the political or military leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That means that I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge, even outside the military and political leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is to say, lower down, at lower levels, that any commander of the police forces, or even leader, not only commander, or leader, komandant, and komandir is the terms we use in our language - komandirs are leaders or commanders of lower-ranking units - that they planned, ordered or instigated any kind of crime? Did you arrive at knowledge of that kind at all? Did any information reach you about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no knowledge of that kind reached me. I have no knowledge of that taking place, and I can say that all the members of the army of Yugoslavia are very well-known, and I assume the members of the police as well are very well aware of what should be done, and even if a crime were to be committed they know what they should do with the perpetrators. Which means I have no knowledge to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were strict orders precisely to the reverse, to protect the civilian population and to investigate any offences and crimes and to take the perpetrators into custody and take them to court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that a moment ago in my response. I forgot to mention the protection of the civilian population which was always the primary concern of all our security forces especially when it came to issuing orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, were you present at least at one of the meetings on any occasion, in fact, when the leaders, and in this case, I mean generals, the generals of the police and other people reporting, when they said that a lot of terrorists were managing to escape precisely because they were intermingling with the civilian population and the police had strict orders not to open fire if the danger existed that by doing so they would harm civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that. I even had occasion to see a written document to that effect. And I think that it's very easy and simple to find documents to that effect in the archives of the army of Yugoslavia. With respect to certain larger movements, I remember a figure of over 3.000 Albanians, for example, who were moving towards the Albanian border, and that assistance and reinforcement was sought from the police of Montenegro as the MUP of Serb did not wish to intervene precisely for the reasons you've just mentioned. Because amongst them it was assumed that there were quite a lot of terrorists who were leaving together with the civilian population. And as far as I remember, it said in that report - and as I say, we can find the report - that the MUP of Montenegro enabled them to pass through safely and securely without fire being opened, despite the fact that there were terrorists among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, as Mr. May will not let me ask you the questions that I had intended to ask you, I should like to take advantage of the time that I have left for my cross-examination to ask you something with regard to the documents pointed out to us by Mr. Nice, referred to by Mr. Nice, and it is the minutes of the Supreme Defence Council meetings when the president of Yugoslavia was Dobrica Cosic. I shall try to pass over it quickly. I'm going to use a different order, perhaps, but we have the Supreme Defence Council meeting of the 8th and 10th of July, 1992, that was one instance. And we can see that the presiding officer was Dobrica Cosic, then that I was present as well as Momir Bulatovic as members of the Supreme Defence Council, the chief of the general staff attended, and so on and so forth. Borislav Jovic, the president of the state committee for cooperation with the UN, who had been previously been a member of the Yugoslavia Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is tab 12. The witness should have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can it be seen from this, Mr. Lilic, does this show already on page 1, before we go over to the agenda, Dr. Borislav Jovic, the president of the federal committee, state committee, for cooperation with the UN forces, then there was Gavro Perazic informing the Supreme Defence Council with the requirements of the UNPROFOR commander forces, General Satish Nambiar, and the basic premises of international law?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a rather bad copy, but I can just make that out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is the conclusion clear, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia fully accepts point 18 of the UN peace operations in Yugoslavia, the deployment of the units of the Yugoslav People's Army outside the area of Croatia after being taken over by UNPROFOR in the zones under the protection of the United Nations. That is to say, it completely accepts this.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the yellow and blue zone, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In point 2, it says: "The withdrawal of the Yugoslavia army will be carried out in accordance with that plan pursuant to the concrete agreement between the Yugoslav army general staff and the UNPROFOR command" that's right, isn't it, there's absolutely no restrictions there and it is being adopted wholly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then we come to point 3 where it says that: "The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia deems that it is in the interests of peace to secure through that agreement that the Croatian forces may not bring heavy armament in to the vicinity of the Yugoslav borders, thus jeopardising its safety or security." And then, as this was a very vital question, when it comes to the Prevlaka, it says: "Given that the area of Prevlaka (the Ostra cape) stretches only for 93 acres, that is to say, less than 1 hectare, and that it is unclear, or rather that it was always an exclusively military zone, that is to say, without any inhabitants. It was uninhabited, an exclusively military zone, and that by its position, it controls the whole of the Bay of Kotor, Boka-Kotorska," and as we know, that belongs to Montenegro, or rather the FRY, that is to say "controls the whole of the bay of Kotor, or rather 30 per cent of the coastline of Yugoslavia, and there are ongoing political negotiations about the rightful demarcation of the economic, sea and epicontinental border between the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia and Croatia. The Yugoslav army may abandon Prevlaka on condition that that territory be placed under the provisional control of the United Nations." That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that the agreement that was reached and it was at that time that the yellow zones and the blue zones came into being? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia will expect" - and this is a very poor copy, so I can hardly read it - "the outcome of political negotiations, and the appropriate decision of the International Court of Justice, as the final solution." And then it goes on to say that an appropriate memorandum be compiled. Now, does this meeting show that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, judging by the Supreme Defence Council meeting, as a whole, adheres to the agreements reached and abides by them fully, with UNPROFOR or rather the representatives of the United Nations, and fully fulfills its obligation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and not only these minutes, but I can safely say that was the policy pursued by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to comment on the second minutes of the 7th of August, because I did not attend that meeting myself. I think there was some discussion about the situation in Plevlja, which is a town in Montenegro, on the territory of Montenegro. However, it is emphasised in this regard, and it's the last paragraph relating to point 1, rather, a decision through energetic activities to end private support by certain Yugoslav army and MUP officers and prevent all threats to property and the personal security of citizens and the encouragement of interethnic intolerance, to prevent all that. "Faithful implementation and positive results will have a far greater impact," it says. And what is referred to is the territory of Montenegro and the problems at the state borders towards Bosnia-Herzegovina and the broader territory in the Plevlja municipality. Now, can we see from this and say quite clearly that Yugoslavia wishes to see the problem solved by peaceful means? Was that the policy pursued?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then we have the 6th session of the 9th of December, 1992. And the first point refers to the threats of military intervention in Bosnia-Herzegovina, possible aggression by Croatia against the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and the possible secessionist Albanian uprising in Kosovo. The situation in the Defence Ministry. "Point 1, introductory report by the president of the FR of Yugoslavia, Dobrica Cosic, drew attention to the current international political situation which threatens a further intensification and deepening of the crisis within the area of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which could have serious consequences for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." And then it mentions a meeting to be held with representatives of the representatives -- leaders of the Srpska Krajina. But I'd like to draw your attention to an important provision. It is to be found in point 2. It is point 1 of point 2. That the army of Yugoslavia is a nonpolitical organisation, and in accordance with its constitutional role, may not become involved in current political activities. It must be over and above political manipulations and may not be subordinated to any party, political platform, or political figures. And then it goes on to say under number 2, the Supreme Defence Council condemns all attempts to introduce a pre-election party political orientation to the Yugoslav army as well as immoderate and tendentious statements by various state officials and party leaders regarding the Yugoslav army. Do you remember that there are many attacks launched against the army and that insistence was made and that there were various party paramilitary formations that were established and that all that, in a way, was a factor of destabilisation? It destabilised the situation, and the Supreme Defence Council was energetic in standing up to that. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a decision dating back to 1992. I haven't got the minutes of the meeting in front of me but I can comment on it because I did see the minutes and remember the minutes and it was a time when the parties entered into competition to see which would be able to attack the Yugoslav army more and others to become infiltrated in the Yugoslav army. And I think this conclusion was respected later on with respect to the paramilitary units. I think, or rather, I'm certain that immediately after I came to the Supreme Defence Council and guided by this conclusion, that an order was issued that all paramilitary units should be disbanded, which were identified as having been in existence at that time. And a decision of that kind by the Supreme Defence Council does exist, and we can always see it if The Hague Tribunal wishes to find it and take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So from all this and from subsequent practice, from the time when you were the president of the FRY yourself, the president of the National Assembly of Serbia, holding the top posts in Yugoslavia and in Serbia, do you know of a single example in which in any way whatsoever anybody whatsoever of the leadership of the official organs strove and advocated the protection of paramilitary formations or anything like that? Or rather, was it quite -- was the policy of Serbia and Yugoslavia quite clear, and that was that under no circumstances should the formation of paramilitaries be allowed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've answered that question a moment ago when I said that there is an official decision by the Supreme Defence Council to prohibit and destroy and eliminate any paramilitary formations. And this is borne out and evidenced by these minutes from the Supreme Defence Council meeting that was chaired by Mr. Dobrica Cosic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to have to bring this session to a close. Mr. Lilic, I'm afraid we're going to have to ask you to come back, require you to do so. We'll try and find a date which is convenient to you, if you could make yourself available. Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, we'll give you another half hour to conclude your cross-examination. You will have had substantially more than the Prosecution. There will be then time for the amicus and for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Your Honour, you'll remember I was asking that the witness could be shown some documents, just to produce them. They've come up today from Belgrade. Is that possible, that we can just lay them before him now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm afraid not today. We have to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the amicus have some questions to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I said the amicus. If I didn't, I meant to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question of how much time to make available, because time is very short and we are having to fit this witness in with other witnesses, my original plan had been to have him come for, I thought it was just going effectively to be a re-examination session, so to come first thing in the morning and to come in 11, 11.30 and to be finished that day. We would much prefer that because we have a great deal of evidence to get through. A lot of witnesses are going to be, as it were, interesting in the way this witness is, but that evidence will have to be focussed by us, and we would ask by the accused. We would prefer -- obviously it would help us if we can know how much time the court was going to allow the amicus because otherwise we're in a slightly open-ended position and don't know what to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Half an hour, Mr. Tapuskovic; would that be sufficient for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what can I say? It would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case, Your Honour, I'll work on the same basis because I'm sure I can conclude what I have to say in 45 minutes or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Effectively, it would be one session. But there is the question of new documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the new documents, the documents we have, I'm not going to deal with extensively or anything like that.
